Highlights
- India's ₹343 billion National Critical Minerals Mission and a separate magnet manufacturing scheme have attracted 20 bidders, but industrial interest does not equal qualified production capacity.
- China controls roughly 90% of rare earth processing, with advantages in engineering talent, equipment, and integrated manufacturing that mineral acquisitions alone cannot replicate.
- India must develop two distinct supply chains—battery materials and rare earth permanent magnets—each requiring different refining, metallurgical, and manufacturing capabilities.
- Democratic complexity, bureaucratic layers, and land acquisition hurdles risk turning India's ambitious industrial programs into years of negotiation and delay.
- REEx recommends tracking commercial recovery rates, metal purity, magnet performance, and customer qualification rather than projected capacity figures.

articles.title: Copper could be the energy transition’s biggest bottleneck: GEM Mining - Mining.com.au
articles.summary: Copper could be the energy transition’s biggest bottleneck: GEM Mining  Mining.com.au
articles.full_text:
The energy transition’s biggest mineral challenge may not be the one the market is watching most closely.
While lithium has dominated critical minerals discussions amid surging demand for electric vehicle (EV) batteries and energy storage, a new analysis from GEM Mining Consulting points to copper as the metal most likely to constrain the energy transition by 2035.
The report, Which metal will be the real bottleneck of the energy transition toward 2035, argues that copper’s importance extends beyond a single technology or market.
Its widespread use across electricity networks, renewable energy infrastructure, and electrification means supply constraints could have consequences across multiple industries.
Compounding the challenge, developing new mines can take years, limiting the industry’s ability to respond quickly to rising demand.
To identify the minerals most likely to constrain the transition, GEM Mining assessed six critical minerals, including copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and magnetic rare earths.
Rather than examining supply and demand alone, the consulting firm evaluated four factors. These include volume pressure, technological breadth, mitigation rigidity, and supply-chain fragility.
These were combined into its proprietary Systemic Bottleneck Index (SBI), scored from zero to 100.
GEM Mining’s findings highlight an important distinction — the mineral facing the largest relative supply shortfall is not always the one posing the greatest systemic risk.
Copper is the systemic bottleneck
GEM Mining reports that copper ranks first, scoring 72.8 points on the SBI. Its ranking reflects a substantial projected supply shortfall and widespread use across electricity grids, renewable energy, EVs, buildings, industry, and data centres.
“A constraint on copper can propagate widely because the metal is not tied to a single technology,” GEM Mining says.
Copper is used in transmission lines and cables, substations, transformers, generators, inverters, buildings, industrial infrastructure, vehicles and charging infrastructure, pumps, motors, and more.
Across these applications, copper’s role as an electrical conductor is difficult to replace without redesigning systems, oversizing components, or accepting additional efficiency losses.
Copper’s use is not only broad but also massive in scale. GEM Mining reports that its refined market is measured in tens of millions of tonnes annually.
“A percentage gap similar to that of a niche metal therefore implies a much greater requirement for projects, capital, infrastructure, and permitting,” the consulting firm notes.
The challenge is not finding more copper. The industry must discover economically viable deposits, secure investment, obtain approvals, and develop the infrastructure needed to bring additional supply online.
Shrinking discoveries raise supply concerns
The scale of copper demand would be challenging enough without a slowdown in new discoveries.
According to MinEx Consulting Managing Director Richard Schodde, the rate of new copper deposit discoveries has halved over the past decade. This follows a 60% decline in funding for grassroots exploration, as previously reported.
JP Morgan’s model paints an even tighter picture, projecting a 330,000-tonne deficit.
Although the forecasts differ, both point to the pressure facing the market as demand grows and new supply struggles to keep pace.
For explorers, this creates an opportunity to help replenish the project pipeline. However, identifying prospective ground is only the first step in addressing a potential structural shortage.
Exploration could replenish copper supply
Despite the slowdown in discoveries highlighted by Schodde, exploration opportunities remain across established mineral provinces and less-explored regions.
In Western Australia, Buxton Resources (ASX:BUX) is advancing two projects with copper and gold exploration potential, namely the Lateron and Madman projects.
Lateron represents a greenfield exploration opportunity, with a 7km² area of remnant magnetised mafic-ultramafic intrusions that suggest mineralisation.
In Q2 2026, the company defined high-priority copper and gold drill targets. Petrological analysis of core fragments from historical drilling confirmed the presence of host rocks supporting favourable copper-gold prospectivity.
Buxton also owns the Madman Project in Western Australia, which the company says is an “exciting new exploration opportunity with the potential to uncover valuable gold and copper deposits”.
The project is considered promising due to its location in an area with known mineralisation, supported by geological and geophysical data, strategic access to infrastructure, and cost-effective exploration.
Recent diamond drilling at Madman is targeting an electromagnetic conductor associated with the interpreted hydrothermal system, which the company describes as a ‘compelling’ target.
Meanwhile, CGN Resources (ASX:CGR) is exploring for copper and other minerals through its Webb and Broadhurst projects in Western Australia.
Webb is considered highly prospective for iron-oxide copper-gold (IOCG)-style mineralisation and nickel sulphide. The company has already shown the potential for diamondiferous kimberlites, discovering the largest kimberlite field in Australia.
Broadhurst is a copper exploration asset under application in the Paterson Province, a metallogenic province that hosts several copper-gold deposits.
Modern data has identified multiple priority targets beneath shallow cover, where structural complexity, favourable lithologies, and geophysical signatures coincide.
While these projects represent potential additions to the exploration pipeline, their significance depends on whether exploration can translate into discoveries and, eventually, economically viable production.
Copper, however, is only one part of the critical minerals equation.
Lithium faces the largest relative supply gap
GEM Mining’s analysis identifies lithium as a different kind of challenge, with a larger relative supply gap but a more developed range of potential supply responses.
Lithium ranked second in GEM Mining’s SBI assessment, scoring 60.8, and represents the largest volumetric bottleneck in the report’s base case.
Its potential constraints are particularly relevant to electric mobility and energy storage sectors, where lithium-ion batteries remain a key technology.
Under the report’s baseline assumptions, existing operations and committed projects cover just 68% of lithium’s primary requirements by 2035.
However, lithium has a broader project pipeline and more possible supply routes than copper, giving the industry more opportunities to respond.
Global lithium production has grown from 9,485 tonnes in 1995 to more than 292,300 tonnes in 2025, according to Our World in Data.
That growth demonstrates the industry’s capacity to expand production, although the projected gap suggests further development will be required to meet future demand.
Among the companies advancing potential new supply are TG Metals (ASX:TG6) and Global Lithium Resources (ASX:GL1), both developing in Western Australia.
Developers target future supply
TG Metals’ Burmeister lithium deposit lies within the Lake Johnston Greenstone Belt, which hosts defined lithium-caesium-tantalum pegmatites — a source of about one-fourth of the world’s lithium production.
The company has submitted a mining lease application for the deposit and has begun diamond drilling to produce spodumene-rich samples for potential direct shipping ore (DSO) customers.
CEO David Selfe says Burmeister has potential to be “the largest DSO open pit lithium development in Australia”.
Burmeister has a resource of 6.7 million tonnes (Mt) @ 1.2% lithium oxide (Li2O), which TG Metals says makes the deposit materially suitable for the DSO market.
Meanwhile, Global Lithium’s Manna Lithium Project is considered the third-largest resource in the Kalgoorlie lithium province.
A Definitive Feasibility Study outlines a post-tax net present value (NPV) of $472 million and an internal rate of return (IRR) of 25.7% for the project. Manna contains a resource of 51.6Mt @ 1% Li2O and a maiden ore reserve of 19.4Mt @ 0.91% Li2O.
In late September, the company entered into a binding scheme implementation deed with Titan Lithium’s Australian subsidiary to be acquired for $333 million.
Global Lithium Managing Director Dianmin Chen says the board has “weighed the certain and immediate value” on offer against the funding requirements and execution risk involved in constructing the Manna project amid continued lithium market volatility.
“In our view, the offer fairly recognises the value and quality of the Manna Lithium Project and the work our team has done to advance the project, and allows shareholders to realise that value in cash today,” Chen says.
To ensure project development continues uninterrupted, Titan will provide a loan facility of up to $120 million across four tranches.
The contrasting positions of these developers illustrate how companies are navigating the lithium market.
Some are progressing towards production, while others are weighing the capital requirements and execution risks of development against opportunities to realise value.

Key Highlights
- Surge Battery Metals is in focus after its latest reported update.
- The next catalysts are execution, additional detail and measurable follow-through.
- Investors should assess funding, dilution, sector conditions and project-specific risks.
- The announcement is not a guarantee of commercial success or share-price performance.
Surge Battery Metals (TSXV:NILI) is in focus following its latest update on critical minerals spotlight: nevada north lithium study reframes development debate. For investors tracking Canadian-listed companies on the TSX Venture Exchange, the key issue is what the announcement changes about the company's operating outlook, funding needs or next milestones. The update is relevant on 16 October 2026 because it gives the market a fresh point to assess execution, risk and the evidence still required before any longer-term investment conclusion can be drawn.
Surge Battery Metals' Nevada North study places lithium development economics and project scale at the centre of the critical-minerals discussion. The study outlines a staged development concept and a long operating horizon, but the substantial capital requirement means funding strategy, construction execution and market assumptions are crucial. Lithium prices can move sharply with supply additions, battery demand and inventory cycles. Investors should test the study's price assumptions, recovery rates, operating costs, permitting timeline, water and infrastructure needs, and the route from feasibility work to a construction decision.
Why is Surge Battery Metals in focus?
The immediate catalyst is the company's reported development, rather than an assumed share-price move. Without verified live trading data in this article, it would be inappropriate to claim that the stock is rising, falling or objectively trending today. The news may nevertheless attract attention because it changes the information set available to investors. The practical question is whether it advances the business beyond an intention or plan and whether the company has supplied enough detail to measure the significance of the event.
What does the update mean for the business?
The announcement should be assessed against the company's stage of development. For an exploration business, the key test is whether new work improves geological understanding and supports the next round of technical decisions. For a development-stage issuer, attention shifts to engineering, permits, capital costs, financing and project schedules. For a consumer or healthcare technology company, adoption, distribution, retention, regulatory considerations and revenue quality matter more than the announcement alone. These distinctions help investors avoid treating very different corporate events as equivalent catalysts.
What should investors watch next?
The next important milestones are likely to include fuller technical or commercial detail, implementation progress, and a clear timetable for follow-up work. Investors should look for measurable evidence: completed work rather than planned work, final agreements rather than preliminary proposals, and published results rather than expectations. Where relevant, the next update should clarify budget, timing, responsible counterparties, approvals and the criteria by which management will judge success. Delays or changes to scope can be just as informative as positive milestones.
Funding, dilution and balance-sheet considerations
Funding is especially important for smaller listed companies because exploration, product development and project construction can consume substantial capital before generating reliable cash flow. Investors should examine cash on hand, expected spending, debt obligations, financing conditions and any potential share issuance. A financing can extend the runway, but it may also dilute existing holders or introduce repayment requirements. A headline commitment should not be treated as cash available until the relevant conditions and closing status are clear.
Sector conditions and the wider market context
Surge Battery Metals's prospects may be influenced by commodity prices, investor risk appetite, interest rates, supply-chain conditions and access to capital. These external forces can affect valuation multiples even when company-specific execution is unchanged. They should be treated as context rather than proof of value. For resource companies, a favourable commodity backdrop cannot eliminate geological, metallurgical, permitting or construction risks. For consumer and technology issuers, market opportunity must translate into customers, margins and sustainable cash generation.
Key risks that could change the outlook
The main risks include weaker-than-expected technical or commercial results, delays, cost overruns, financing uncertainty, regulatory or permitting issues, and changes in market conditions. Early-stage projects carry additional uncertainty because targets may not become resources and resources may not become economically recoverable reserves. Announced partnerships, study outcomes and plans also depend on assumptions that can change. Investors should review the company's own detailed disclosure before relying on headline summaries, and should distinguish management expectations from independently demonstrated outcomes.
How to interpret the next announcement
A useful follow-up release should add information rather than simply repeat the original headline. For Surge Battery Metals, investors can ask whether the next update resolves an open question, quantifies progress, reduces uncertainty or identifies a new constraint. Comparisons with prior guidance can show whether management is delivering on its stated timetable. Where technical metrics are reported, grade, width, scale, recovery, cost and assumptions should be read together rather than in isolation. Where commercial metrics are relevant, revenue quality, gross margin, customer acquisition costs and cash generation deserve attention.
Investor outlook for 16 October 2026
The latest development places Surge Battery Metals on investors' watchlists, but the longer-term impact depends on follow-through. A constructive interpretation would require evidence that the announcement advances the project or business, is adequately funded and can be translated into measurable progress. A cautious interpretation is warranted where key terms remain preliminary, technical data are incomplete or further financing is likely. Investors should avoid treating attention around a news event as a substitute for valuation work, risk assessment or a review of the company's complete disclosures.

articles.title: Critical minerals: Why mining communities may suffer the fate of Niger Delta - The Sun Nigeria
articles.summary: Critical minerals: Why mining communities may suffer the fate of Niger Delta  The Sun Nigeria
articles.full_text:
As Nigerians await the report of the panel set up to investigate the circumstances that led to the avoidable death of 37 artisanal miners in Niger State, it has become imperative to examine the desperation for critical minerals by non-states actors and countries like China, EU, and the US. In doing so, it is also pertinent to understand why the minerals are “critical.” A publication of the Belfer Centre for Science and International Affairs reveals the three conditions stipulated by the U.S. Energy Act of 2020 that make a mineral to be termed critical. One, the mineral has to be “essential to economic or national security.” Two, “its supply chain is vulnerable to disruption,” and three, “it performs a function in manufacturing that cannot be replaced without serious consequences, whether higher costs for key technologies, slower deployment of clean energy, or risks to defense and communications systems.”
There is another dimension that further underlines the critical element. The geopolitics of where the mineral is mined can make it critical especially, “if it is refined or processed elsewhere, particularly by a strategic rival. An example of this is China’s dominance in rare earth refining,” the Belfer Center noted. Hence, China’s likelihood of withholding supply to gain advantage is a cause for worry.
Some of these critical minerals which are inextricably connected to global transition to clean energy, production of national defense gadgetsn and artificial intelligence data storage, include copper, cobalt, lithium, manganese, graphite, nickel, rare earth elements and platinum group metals (PGMs). And to follow the momentum, advanced nations continue to update their lists of critical minerals based on technological discoveries and growing appetite for them. Already, estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA) as captured in Jordy Lee Calderon’s article in Milken Institute Review made a projection that the world “will require six times more mineral inputs for renewable technologies in 2040 than today,” just as the “Demand for lithium to manufacture rechargeable electricity storage, for example, is expected to increase at least 20-fold.”
In terms of global distribution, the highest reserves of critical minerals are unevenly spread across the leading nations of China, Australia, the Lithium Triangle region – (Chile, Argentina and Bolivia), Indonesia, as well as African countries like the Democratic of Congo (DRC), South Africa, Gabon, and Guinea. There are other countries in Africa including Nigeria that have significant deposits of critical minerals, but DRC alone has almost 75% of global cobalt reserves.
Meanwhile, with roughly 30% of global reserves of critical minerals, Africa is at the centre of strategic engagements for global supply, but unfortunately, the continent lacks the technical and technological capabilities to refine the minerals locally.
What is therefore witnessed in the continent is mostly raw extraction for exports by artisanal miners, factions and fractions of criminal cartels of the elites, as well as some powerful officials in government who exploit the weak regulatory environment to rip off their countries.
As such, the continent has inadvertently turned into battlegrounds for all manner of indigenous and external interests, with the mining sector morphing into a new rent-seeking frontier in Africa.
The 80% control of critical minerals processing and refining by China has also awoken the U.
S.
from passivity.
The irony, according to Calderon, is that it was the U.
S.
that “invented the complex industrial processes used for separating rare earth elements decades ago, then ceded production to China.
” For years, the U.
S.
and some other industrialized nations looked down on mining and metals industry, and China dominated the space.
But lately, the U.
S.
is poised to square up to China by extending its tentacles to African critical minerals sector.
The U.
S.
and E.
U.
have brokered deals to secure supplies from Africa.
And with Chinese companies already operating in some regions in Africa, including Nigeria, the battle may not be in the interest of the continent if they fail to act together.

The major challenge is that the mining sector in Africa is not strongly regulated amid the “new scramble”. Nigeria is still playing politics by pampering the big illegal miners who became billionaires overnight without verifiable economic production. Beyond that, Abraham Nunbogu and Kaveh Madani of Institute for Water, Environment and Health, United Nations University have raised concerns about creating “sacrifice zones” with the enormous amounts of water needed for minerals extraction and the health hazards in host communities in Africa and South America. They noted that, “In 2024 alone, global lithium production required an estimated 456 billion litres of water. That is equivalent to the annual domestic water needs of roughly 62 million people in sub‑Saharan Africa. At the same time, much of the world is facing water bankruptcy, meaning people and industries are using more fresh water than nature can replenish, leading to irrecoverable ecosystem damages.”
Besides, the communities close to the extraction sites have reportedly suffered “skin diseases, gastrointestinal illnesses, reproductive health problems and chronic health conditions associated with long‑term exposure to heavy metals in polluted water and soil…Evidence from mining regions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is particularly stark. Studies document high rates of miscarriages, congenital malformations and infant mortality among populations exposed to environments contaminated with cobalt and other metals,” as noted by Nunbogu and Madani. The mining communities in Nigeria are also having their sad tales.
Indeed, Nigeria and other African nations are not doing enough to stop industrialized nations from eating their lunch. And if care is not taken, the continent will relapse into another round of “resource curse.” Efforts should be made to ensure that the resource wealth is used in a sustainable manner by negotiating as a team under a continental platform instead of doing it by individual countries. Agreements should prioritise skills development, local content, and a clear-cut plan for closure of mining sites after exploration. Nigeria should understudy how Norway made its hydrocarbon resources work for the present and future generations. Let Nigeria avoid another environmental despoilation occasioned by mining without responsibility like the Niger Delta.

articles.title: Major development banks step up support for critical minerals value chains - Mining.com
articles.summary: Major development banks step up support for critical minerals value chains  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Multilateral development banks (MDBs) will strengthen efforts to help mineral-rich developing economies add more value to their resources by moving beyond extraction into processing, refining and manufacturing, according to an outline of a critical minerals collaboration framework published on Saturday.
The banks involved include the World Bank, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the European Investment Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, according to the outline.
The October framework calls for coordinated support across critical mineral supply chains, including financing, infrastructure and policy aimed at creating jobs, boosting domestic value addition, attracting private investment and supporting low-carbon transition.
MDBs plan to support mineral corridors incorporating power, transport, logistics, water and digital infrastructure, while strengthening project preparation and using co-financing, guarantees and other financing tools to mobilise capital and accelerate private sector investments.
They will also seek closer alignment on environmental and social standards, coordinate support to governments and better connect mining projects with infrastructure and industrial development.
An MDB working group will coordinate implementation of the framework’s objectives and report annually to the Heads of MDBs Group on progress.
(Reporting by Karen Lema; Editing by Tom Hogue)

articles.title: "Why discard spent batteries?" Lithium and nickel are pouring out... A wave of 'love calls' to POSCO - 머니투데이
articles.summary: "Why discard spent batteries?" Lithium and nickel are pouring out... A wave of 'love calls' to POSCO  머니투데이
articles.full_text:
Lithium and nickel pour out from POSCO factory... Over 90% of used batteries are re-resourcized
"Ta0"① Reborn as critical minerals"Tb0"
On Sept. 17, upon entering a large raw material warehouse inside the 19,000-pyeong-scale POSCOHY Clean Metal factory located in the Yulchon Industrial Complex in Gwangju, South Jeonnam Province, over 1,000 sacks (ton bags) containing black powder caught our attention.
Packed tightly within these sacks is "black mass," produced by crushing used batteries and scrap generated during the battery manufacturing process. As one sack hooked onto a crane was lifted above the raw material input port, the black powder poured out. Production equipment connected via piping began processing it. This is the first step in discarded batteries being reborn as critical minerals.
Black mass is a black powder containing critical minerals such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese. Because it can be reused as battery material after undergoing recycling processes, it is considered a key raw material for "urban mines." POSCOHY Clean Metal utilizes 12,000 tons of black mass annually to produce 2,500 tons of lithium carbonate, 12,000 tons of nickel sulfate, 3,800 tons of cobalt sulfate, and 2,000 tons of manganese sulfate.
The recovered valuable metals are sufficient to produce over 60,000 electric vehicles. Kim Ho-young, Gyeong Yeong-gi-hoek (Head) at POSCOHY Clean Metal, emphasized, "The recovery rate for major valuable metals is over 90%, and the quality non-conformance rate is less than 0.1%, representing a globally top-tier level."
The recycling of used batteries is becoming increasingly important in tandem with the restructuring of global supply chains. This is because movements to reduce dependence on Chinese critical minerals are spreading, and demand for recycled metals is increasing as tax credit requirements have been strengthened under the U.S. Prohibited Foreign Institutional Investor (PFE) regulations. This is why domestic companies such as Hyundai Motor Group, LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On are accelerating efforts to build a used battery resource circulation system.
As used batteries emerge as a new source of supply, the Lisa cycle market is also expected to grow. According to market research firm SNE Research, global used battery generation is projected to increase from 44 GWh (gigawatt-hours) in 2025 to 3,339 GWh by 2040. This represents a surge of approximately 76 times over 15 years.
The market size is also expected to reach approximately 230 trillion won by 2040. Lee Hang-gu, a special professor at Seoul National University, stated, "It is a means not only for waste treatment but also for reducing overseas dependence on critical minerals, stabilizing supply chains, and securing cost competitiveness."
POSCO, which has built a mineral business supply chain through 'Lisa cycling'... How it contributes to the circular economy [Report]
"Ta0"② Visiting POSCOHY Clean Metal"Tb0"
"POSCOHY Clean Metal is responsible for Lisa cycling, the final button in the POSCO Group's secondary battery material value chain (value chain), and is a core company completing the 'Resource Circulation System (Closed Loop).'"
Kim Ho-young, chief of management planning division, whom we met at the POSCOHY Clean Metal factory located in the Yulchon Industrial Complex in Gwangju, South Jeonnam Province on the 17th of last month, stated, "We are playing a key role as part of the 'indispensable resource security company' and 'supply chain guardian' that the group aims to be."
He further revealed pride in the battery recycling business, saying, "It is highly significant that we produce raw materials to replace critical secondary battery materials that our country, which lacks natural resources, relies on imports for."
POSCOHY Clean Metal is the only domestic company that recovers critical minerals from used batteries and manufacturing scrap to produce high-quality lithium carbonate, nickel sulfate, cobalt sulfate, manganese sulfate, as well as Busan substances such as copper, all within a single factory. Director Kim emphasized, "Since the production of initial products in May 2023, we have increased our operating rate, which currently exceeds 95%."
He also answered why the POSCO Group entered the battery recycling business while directly securing critical minerals such as lithium and nickel from overseas mines and salt lakes.
Kim explained, "If mineral procurement through mines and salt lakes is the 'axis of large-scale raw material procurement' to respond to the surge in demand for core raw materials, then Lisa cycling is the axis of resource virtuous circulation and supply chain stability," adding that "recycled raw materials play an important role in securing cost competitiveness."
The POSCO Group is building a supply chain spanning from mines to battery material production and recycling through its affiliates. Nickel secured from Western Australia and other regions is processed into nickel sulfate through its own supply chain connected to affiliates.
In fact, graphite secured from mines in Tanzania and Australia is utilized as anode material raw material, while coal tar is transformed into needle coke and pitch at POSCO MC Materials. These raw materials are also fed into the production of precursors, cathode materials, and anode materials by POSCO Future M.
Recycling will play a role in completing the supply chain within the group. POSCO Holdings operates a pre-treatment subsidiary (PLSC) for black mass (black powder containing critical minerals such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese) in Poland.
The black mass produced there is supplied to domestic POSCOHY Clean Metal. Subsequently, through post-processing, it is refined into lithium, nickel, cobalt, and manganese, and then supplied to domestic and overseas companies such as POSCO Future M. In this way, POSCOHY Clean Metal serves as the final button in the resource circulation system.
Kim conveyed, "Visits from companies seeking recycled minerals produced in non-China supply chains have continued, allowing us to feel a year-on-year increase in demand." He added, "Battery and finished vehicle manufacturers in the U.S. and Japan are making inquiries, and European finished vehicle manufacturers are also visiting factories to discuss cooperation."
The successive love calls from global companies show that recycled raw materials are emerging as strategic resources. The U.S. has restricted the overseas export of black mass and tungsten waste/scrap since August 27 last year. It mandates priority supply to domestic purchasers and allows overseas sales only in cases where prior exception approval has been granted. POSCOHY Clean Metal is currently conducting negotiations for such exception approval.
This is in the same context as Jang In-hwa, Chairman of the POSCO Group, previously proposing a "Triple Core" strategy that designates steel, secondary battery material minerals, and energy resources as three core businesses, declaring an initiative to strengthen national industrial security and supply chains.
Kim stated, "In Korea, where minerals are not mined, producing critical minerals through recycling and contributing to the transition from a mining economy to a circular economy is the direction that the group and the company aim for."

articles.full_text:
Enbridge just kicked off a non-binding open season to test commercial interest in a proposed natural gas pipeline expansion — one that would connect the Katy Hub in Texas to southwest Louisiana. The solicitation runs from October 7 through October 30, giving prospective customers a window to submit transportation requests before the company decides whether to push the project forward. Enbridge is proposing a transportation arrangement that utilizes capacity on the Mustang Express Pipeline system.
Enbridge opens market solicitation for Gulf Coast pipeline project
An open season is a standard industry move. It lets potential customers signal how much pipeline capacity they’d want to reserve before anyone commits to building anything — essentially a structured market test before writing big checks.
During that window, prospective customers can submit formal transportation requests that tell Enbridge whether enough commercial demand exists to justify moving forward. Without sufficient interest, the project stalls.
Gulf Coast LNG export capacity has grown significantly in recent years, and moving gas out of the country at scale means moving it through pipelines first.
The proposed arrangement utilizing capacity on the Mustang Express Pipeline is central to how the expansion would actually work. It combines infrastructure from two separate pipeline systems to create a more connected route between Texas and Louisiana — which is the whole point.
Why Enbridge is pursuing the expansion
The logic here is pretty direct: natural gas demand in southwest Louisiana is growing, and existing infrastructure may not be enough to keep up.
The proposed expansion would combine transportation services on the Mustang Express and Texas Eastern pipeline systems — a pairing that makes the routing viable by linking the Katy Hub to Gulf Coast markets that increasingly need supply. The Katy Hub is a major Texas trading and distribution point, and one of the most important natural gas hubs in North America.
Much of that need traces back to LNG export activity. Gulf Coast LNG export capacity has grown significantly in recent years, and moving gas out of the country at scale means moving it through pipelines first. Industrial growth and power generation demand along the Gulf Coast add pressure on top of that. The region isn’t just exporting more — it’s consuming more too.
Expected benefits and target markets
Enbridge says the expansion would improve connectivity between Texas supply sources and Louisiana demand centers — a corridor that’s becoming more strategically important as Gulf Coast energy infrastructure scales up.
On the LNG side, the project would enhance access to export facilities along the US Gulf Coast. As more terminals come online or expand, the pipelines feeding them need to keep pace, and a direct, high-capacity connection from the Katy Hub to southwest Louisiana addresses that gap.
Beyond LNG, the project would serve industrial customers and power generators in the region. These aren’t small sectors — Gulf Coast industrial facilities rank among the largest natural gas consumers in the country, and power generators in the area have seen demand rise alongside population and economic growth.
Stack LNG exports on top of industrial load and power generation, and southwest Louisiana becomes one of the more compelling markets for new pipeline capacity in North America right now. Enbridge’s project is essentially a bet that this demand isn’t going away.
Next steps and project timeline
The open season is just the first step in a longer process. Even with strong commercial interest, there’s still a lot that has to happen before construction begins.
Enbridge first needs to secure sufficient commercial support by the October 30 deadline. If the transportation requests don’t add up to enough demand, the project doesn’t advance — at least, not in its current form. Regulatory approvals come next, since pipeline projects at this scale require sign-off from relevant authorities before any ground breaks. Companies typically run open seasons precisely because they want to confirm market demand before investing in that regulatory process.
If both conditions are met, Enbridge is targeting an early 2031 in-service date. That’s roughly five years out, which tracks with the typical timeline for a project this complex: open season, regulatory filings, approvals, construction, commissioning.
What this project adds up to
Enbridge is making a calculated move. The non-binding open season — open October 7, closing October 30 — is the company’s way of checking whether the market agrees with its read on Gulf Coast demand before committing real capital.
The project would link the Katy Hub to southwest Louisiana by combining the Mustang Express and Texas Eastern pipeline systems, a route designed to serve LNG export facilities, industrial customers, and power generators in a region where all three are expanding.
Whether it advances comes down to two things: enough transportation requests from prospective customers, and the necessary regulatory approvals. Clear both hurdles, and Enbridge is aiming to have the expansion in service by early 2031. The next meaningful signal arrives after October 30, when the open season closes, and the company can see what the market actually said.

articles.title: Part 2 – RBAC Inc.: The biggest natural gas pipeline projects you should know in 2026 - World Pipelines

In Part 1, we looked at major pipeline developments in North America and Europe. North America is seeing large new pipelines built around takeaway capacity for growing production and feeding both LNG exports and power demand, while Europe is increasingly focused on expanding, reversing and improving infrastructure connections already in place.
Part 2 takes us into the Middle East, Asia-Pacific, South America and Africa, where projects vary greatly in size and scope, and could reshape regional or even global gas trade, but still depend on political agreements, pricing, security or financing. This is particularly true of megaprojects such as Power of Siberia 2, TAPI, Trans-Saharan and African Atlantic gas pipelines.
When we ask how likely, we can ask do the projects have clear supply, demand, financing and construction schedules? As discussed in Part 1, the question is what problem does the pipeline solve, what supply and demand sit at either end, and how likely is it to actually operate at or near significant capacity?
We begin in the Middle East, where some of the most important pipeline investments are motivated by rapidly changing domestic gas needs, rather than by LNG exports.
Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean
The Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean contain some interesting examples where domestic consumption, regional trade and LNG exports are drivers for new pipelines.
Saudi Arabia’s Master Gas System Phase Three (expected 2028)
Saudi Aramco’s mega project is ~4000 km of pipeline and 17 new compression trains that will move an additional 3.15 billion ft3/d across the Kingdom by 2028, bringing more Saudi-produced gas to power plants, industrial users and petrochemical facilities. Jafurah gas field is a major supply source and its development has been touted as the Middle East’s own Shale Revolution. Jafurah holds an estimated 200-plus trillion ft3 of gas and is one of the largest unconventional gas developments outside North America.
The project was already part of Aramco’s long-running gas expansion strategy rather than driven by the Iran conflict; however, recent regional instability and concerns around Gulf export chokepoints make its strategic rationale stronger: more domestic gas production, less oil burn in power generation, larger internal transportation networks and greater system resilience all become more valuable when maritime chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz are under threat.
Israel – Egypt Expansion Systems (2026 - 2029)
Chevron and its partners gave the go-ahead for a US$2.36 billion Phase 1B expansion in January 2026 to raise Leviathan’s production from 12 to 21 billion m3/y by 2029. But near-term flows are also already increasing: Leviathan added a third gathering line, while Israel Natural Gas Lines completed the 46 km Ashdod–Ashkelon subsea loop along Israel’s southern Mediterranean coast in July 2026. The loop connects into the East Mediterranean Gas (EMG) pipeline, which crosses from Ashkelon to El-Arish in Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula, and lifts EMG capacity from 6.5 - 8.5 billion m3/y.
The Nitzana pipeline, scheduled for late 2028, will provide another route into Egypt. The 65 km overland line will cross Israel’s Negev Desert from the Ramat Hovav area to the Nitzana border crossing, adding roughly 600 million ft3/d of capacity and supporting Leviathan’s US$35 billion, 130 billion m3 supply contract with Egypt’s Blue Ocean Energy.
In the short term, higher Israeli pipeline imports can help Egypt offset its domestic production decline and reduce LNG imports. Longer term, if Egypt’s domestic balance improves, additional Israeli gas could find its way to the Idku and Damietta LNG export facilities and strengthening Egypt’s role as a regional gas and LNG hub.
Cyprus – Egypt Offshore Gas Connections (2028 - 2031)
Cyprus and Egypt are proposing two subsea pipeline projects that would connect offshore Cypriot gas directly with Egypt’s existing processing and LNG infrastructure.
Cronos (Expected 2028) is now the more commercially advanced project. Eni and TotalEnergies took FID on 28 July 2026 for the Block 6 development south of Cyprus. Four deepwater wells will send gas by subsea pipeline to Egypt’s existing Zohr offshore infrastructure, which will carry it to shore and ultimately to the Damietta LNG plant on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast. Production is targeted for 2028 at 500 million ft3/d, equivalent to about 2.8 million tpy of LNG, with Eni and TotalEnergies each marketing half of the volumes.
Aphrodite (planned; expected 2030 - 2031) would create a second Cyprus–Egypt route. Chevron, Shell and NewMed plan to send gas from the field southeast of Cyprus through a new subsea pipeline to Port Said, Egypt. The partners and Egypt’s EGAS are working to finalize commercial agreements in 2026, while front-end engineering design (FEED, the detailed engineering work before an investment decision) continues. The project currently targets FID in the first half of 2027 and production around 2030 - 2031.
Together, the projects could help Cyprus monetize offshore discoveries without building its own LNG export terminal, while providing Egypt additional gas for domestic use or LNG exports when its supply-demand balance permits.
Asia-Pacific: The biggest what ifs
The largest potential – the most challenging
Asia-Pacific contains the projects with the largest potential to change global LNG competition, but also the widest gaps between political announcements and financial execution.
Russia – China Pipeline routes: Power of Siberia 1 & 2 and the Far Eastern route
Russia supplied approximately 38.8 billion m3 through Power of Siberia 1 in 2025, slightly exceeding its original 38 billion m3/y contractual level. The parties have also agreed to increase Power of Siberia 1 deliveries to 44 billion m3/y, reinforcing the route as a core part of China’s overland gas supply.
The Russia–China Far Eastern Route is scheduled to begin deliveries in January 2027 and has been increased from 10 to 12 billion m3/y. It is tied into the Sakhalin – Khabarovsk – Vladivostok system and serves Northeast China, entering its domestic network at Hulin, about 300 km northeast of Vladivostok, its main impact is likely to be regional supply diversity and marginal LNG-import displacement in northern coastal markets.
Power of Siberia 2 is different. Russia, China and Mongolia are reported to have signed a legally binding memorandum in 2025 for a 50 billion m3/y route through Mongolia, including the Soyuz Vostok transit segment, but without pricing, investment terms and the start of deliveries resolved, the legally binding memorandum is not much more than paper. One CNPC researcher said the project would require “tremendous work” and could take eight to ten years. Currently, RBAC’s Base Case assumes a start of 2035, and that could change as the prices, volumes and timeline get closer to finalization.
Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline, Line D
Line A, B and C together with a capacity of 55 billion m3/y are currently transporting gas from Turkmenistan through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to Xinjiang, China. Line D is designed to deliver 30 billion m3/y from Turkmenistan to western China via Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan, bypassing Kazakhstan. Upstream supply prospects were reinforced in April 2026 when Turkmenistan launched Phase 4 of the Galkynysh field expansion which is a US$5.1 billion project under a CNPC turnkey contract to supply 10 billion m3/y. However, the pipeline route itself remains stalled due to unresolved transit terms and long-term pricing agreements. Almost as massive as Power of Siberia 1, it illustrates the fact that China “has options.” The Central Asian region itself has its own fuel challenges domestically with the war in Ukraine reducing Russian energy capacity, and such shortages caused unrest in Kazakhstan in 2022, illustrating the risks in building pipelines through the region.
TAPI – South Asian megaproject
The Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India (TAPI) pipeline is still one of Asia’s biggest “what ifs.” At full design, it would move 33 billion m3/y of Turkmen gas from Galkynysh to Afghanistan, Pakistan and India, with Pakistan and India intended to take roughly 47.5% each and Afghanistan about 5%. At 33 billion m3/y, it is another megaproject that would be a huge boon for Turkmenistan, provide Pakistan and India with long-duration pipeline gas displacing some LNG or coal demand, and turn Afghanistan into a transit and local-gas market rather than a route risk. Afghanistan’s Ministry of Mines and Petroleum reported in July 2026 progress in Afghanistan border-to-Herat section: 101 km of pipeline had been laid, 126 km of corridor prepared, and 36 km buried underground on the Herat section.
Great for Afghanistan, but the larger project still faces familiar challenges; particularly, souring relations between the two anchor buyers, India and Pakistan, and difficult security conditions through southern Afghanistan, non-recognition of the Taliban by Western countries, complicating Western financing, not to mention unresolved downstream commercial commitments, tariff and cost agreements.
Without resolving those, TAPI would become a localised Turkmenistan – Afghanistan supply link under construction, rather than a South Asian mega-project, impacting international gas balances. Another possibility (more realistic) would be TAP. It could possibly be built to connect to Pakistan’s system and then add India later.
South America: the very alive Vaca Muerta
South America’s most important gas pipeline story is centred on Argentina. Venezuela making political headlines in January, has enormous resource potential, but meaningful growth will take time. Brazil has a large gas market and significant offshore resources. Eight governments have announced country partnerships and compacts with the World Bank Group to advance metals and minerals development, expand local supply chains, and bolster critical infrastructure.
The initiative brings together Argentina, Bolivia, Egypt, India, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mauritania, and Zambia to establish measurable targets for modernising mineral licensing, streamlining geological data, strengthening environmental and social oversight, and expanding energy and transport infrastructure.
To back the strategy, the World Bank Group plans to scale its support for the sector fivefold to US$19 billion ($27.3 billion) between FY26 and FY30.
The multilateral program combines policy advice and public financing from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), private capital mobilisation from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), and risk guarantees from the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA).
In South America, Argentina will focus on policy strengthening, provincial coordination, and strategic infrastructure to develop its copper and lithium resources.
Bolivia’s compact modernises its legal framework while introducing a new Investment Bill and Mining Law to drive long-term private investment.
In North Africa and West Asia, Egypt is targeting a 6% minerals contribution to GDP by 2030 and US$9.8 billion in metals and minerals-related exports by 2040 through processing hubs and digital systems.
India intends to mobilise US$5 billion in capital through 2031 to build rare-earth corridors, critical-mineral processing parks, and recycling infrastructure.
Kazakhstan is looking at deploying up to US$20 billion by 2031 via legal reforms, digital geological data, and processing investments.
Across Africa, Malawi will be prioritising mineral licensing transparency, infrastructure development, and workforce expansion.
Mauritania plans to establish pathways for low-emission mineral value creation linked directly to renewable energy.
Finally, Zambia is aiming for annual copper production of 3 million tonnes by 2031 under its Grow Zambia Agenda.
MIGA Managing Director Tsutomu Yamamoto says metals and minerals “make modern life possible”, noting that the World Bank Group works with countries to ensure the sector generates “positive development impact for host countries and local communities”.
“These plans put measurable outcomes behind national ambitions. Success will be judged by whether mineral development creates jobs, strengthens local economies, and expands opportunity — while protecting people and the environment,” Yamamoto says.

articles.title: Critical minerals: The elements of innovation - U.S. National Science Foundation (.gov)

articles.full_text:
These minerals are the backbone of the modern world, powering energy systems, defense technologies, advanced manufacturing, the digital economy, and breakthrough technological innovations.
The bottom line
- Critical minerals are resources like lithium, gallium, and rare earth elements that are in high demand and used to make many of the technologies people rely on every day.
- From smartphones and satellites to medical devices and defense systems, critical minerals underpin key industries, drive technological innovation, and support national security.
- For decades, the U.S. National Science Foundation has invested in the science behind critical minerals, enabling breakthroughs that strengthen U.S. supply chains and industrial capacity.
What are critical minerals?
Critical minerals are naturally occurring elements, minerals, and materials essential to U.S. economic prosperity and national security but are vulnerable to global supply disruptions and difficult to replace.
Whether a mineral is considered critical can change with time as technologies advance, industries evolve, and global supply chains shift. This means a mineral considered critical today may not be in the future, while others may emerge as increasingly vital.
Using the criteria established by the "Energy Act of 2020," the U.S. Geological Survey identified 60 critical mineral commodities in 2025, such as copper, neodymium, aluminum, uranium, cobalt, silver, and platinum group elements.
Why are critical minerals important?
Critical minerals are the raw materials and catalysts needed to produce the technologies and products we rely on every day. For example:
- Smartphones and computers: Tantalum helps capacitors manage electrical current, indium enables touchscreens, and rare earths are used in speakers and vibrant displays.
- Semiconductors and microchips: Silicon, gallium, and germanium are used to make computer chips and other high-performance microelectronics.
- Batteries and energy storage: Lithium, cobalt, nickel, and graphite are key components of rechargeable batteries used in everything from electronics to grid-scale storage.
- Medical technologies: Titanium gives artificial joints strength and durability, platinum supports pacemaker function, and rare earths power high-strength magnets in MRI scanners.
- Fertilizers: Phosphate and potash supply essential nutrients for plant growth and increase global crop yields.
- Defense and aerospace technologies: Aluminum keeps aircraft frames lightweight, rhenium fortifies heat-resistant engines, and rare earths support precision guidance systems and advanced radar sensors.
NSF's investments in critical minerals
For over 75 years, NSF has invested in the science, tools, and talent behind critical minerals, supporting foundational research in geosciences, chemistry, engineering, and materials science. This includes:
- Locating mineral sources: Over decades, NSF-supported research has deepened understanding of where critical minerals are found, how deposits form, and which geological processes influence their distribution. This long-term effort has helped shape modern mineral exploration strategies and improved resource management.
- Recovery and purification: Through sustained investment in separation technologies, including physical, chemical, electrochemical, and biological methods, NSF has continually enhanced the efficiency, selectivity, and versatility of critical mineral recovery. These innovations have enabled the extraction and purification of valuable elements from both ore deposits and secondary waste streams (e.g., mining tailings, wastewater, electronic scrap) and have supported the refinement of high-quality materials essential for modern technology.
- Reducing reliance: NSF-backed research has explored earth-abundant materials, catalysis, substitution chemistry, and advanced manufacturing, yielding viable alternatives for rare earth elements in batteries and magnets that help reduce supply risks while meeting industrial performance demands. Learn more about NSF investments in materials science.
NSF has also supported generations of scientists, engineers, and technical workers across all career stages. Undergraduate research, graduate fellowships, and programs such as Advanced Technical Education give students opportunities to build foundational knowledge and specialized skills, from analyzing crystal chemistry or tectonic structures to locate economic deposits to hands-on training in critical mineral processing, extraction, and recycling technologies. Beyond academia, NSF-supported internships and university-industry partnerships have provided students and researchers with the chance to work alongside mining and industry professionals, gaining practical experience tailored to current industry standards and technical hiring needs.
What opportunities remain?
Demand is increasing, while many critical mineral resources are difficult or expensive to locate, recover, and process.
Meeting that demand will require:
- Finding new sources beyond conventional mining, including wastewater, industrial runoff, geothermal fluids, and mining waste.
- Improving recovery and separation methods so critical minerals can be extracted more efficiently from ores, waste streams, and other materials. This is especially important for rare earth elements, which can be difficult and costly to separate but are essential to technologies such as permanent magnets and electronics.
- Improving recycling so more critical minerals can be recovered from products already in circulation, including discarded electronics.
Taking critical mineral research into the future
From emerging technologies to regional innovation, NSF investments are expanding how researchers discover, understand, and develop critical mineral resources. Projects are revealing how rare earth elements become concentrated in deeply weathered rocks in Georgia's Coastal Plain and how magma evolution and ancient fault systems shaped the Colorado Mineral Belt and Arizona's copper mining district, which may point to promising new exploration targets. In Oklahoma, NSF funding is supporting the development of novel technologies to recover critical minerals from mature shale reservoirs using existing oil and gas infrastructure.
NSF researchers are also exploring new pathways across the mineral life cycle — such as developing a new cobalt mine in Idaho; recovering antimony, nickel, and other critical elements from existing mining operations; and extracting valuable materials from mine waste and industrial wastewater. Other projects, like OneMineralogy, are expanding the world's largest global mineral database and building new analytical tools to accelerate super intelligence-driven discoveries, support mineral exploration and strengthen science education.
NSF also supports research infrastructure that brings together universities, industry and regional partners to cultivate a skilled workforce and address critical mineral needs. For example, the NSF Industry-University Cooperative Research Centers (NSF IUCRC) are advancing geoscience data use in the mining industry and developing methods to recover and recycle critical minerals from electronic waste. Through the NSF Regional Innovation Engines (NSF Engines) initiative, NSF is expanding the domestic supply of critical minerals and materials by supporting new mineral development in Alaska, resource recovery in the Great Lakes, and enhancing materials production in Kansas City. Other NSF efforts, such as the Tech Metal Transformation Challenge, are helping to accelerate breakthrough technologies that will strengthen the U.S. supply chain for critical and strategic metals that power America's energy, defense, and manufacturing future.
As technologies evolve and resource needs continue to change, NSF's sustained investments are helping build the knowledge, capabilities, and talent needed to keep the United States at the forefront of discovery, strengthen domestic supply chains, and support long-term economic competitiveness and national resilience.

This NSF Engine combines advanced mining, processing, and purification technologies to unlock Alaska's mineral potential.

European Commission Picks New Critical Mineral Projects
Another 46 projects have been added to the European Commission's (EC's) fast-growing list of strategic critical minerals projects as it seeks to reduce its reliance on China and others.
Released Monday, October 19, 2026
Written by Martin Lynch, European News Editor for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)
Summary
Another 46 projects have been added to the European Commission's (EC's) fast-growing list of strategic critical minerals projects as it seeks to reduce its reliance on China and others.
Boosting Critical Minerals
The European Commission (EC) has added 46 projects to its rapidly growing list of strategic critical minerals projects.
The winning projects, chosen from 102 that applied, will benefit from strategic project status which includes streamlined permitting, support in accessing financing and assistance in connecting suppliers and buyers. The Commission said the projects are essential to the European Union (EU) not having to rely heavily on other countries for many of these materials, principally China. It added that this dependence has already been used against the EU by limiting their supplies on the open market, which has impacted EU companies' ability to source them. The new projects include seven for lithium, 12 for nickel, 10 for cobalt, five for manganese, and four for graphite, all of which "support the EU battery value chain." The two projects related to magnesium and three for tungsten will contribute to defence and aerospace, while the four projects for rare earth elements will "support the permanent magnet value chain," the EC stated. According to Industrial Info Resources data, there are 11 lithium extraction projects in Europe worth almost US$1.3 billion in investment.
Scope of Projects
The projects cover different stages of the raw materials value chain: eight involve extraction, 11 are for processing, and 19 are recycling projects. In addition, there are eight integrated projects: three that combine extraction and processing, and five that combine processing and recycling. The projects cover 15 of the 17 strategic raw materials under the EU's Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) that mandates that by 2030 EU capacity meets at least 10% of its annual consumption for extraction, 40% for processing and 25% for recycling.
"With this second wave of strategic projects, Europe is stepping up its efforts like never before to reclaim its sovereignty over critical raw materials," said Stéphane Séjourné, executive vice-president for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy at the EC. "Since the adoption of RESourceEU, we have been using every means at our disposal to open mines, develop our processing and recycling capacities, and secure our supply chains. Our approach is simple: reduce dependency, increase production in Europe. We have the resources, the projects and the funding: now we are picking up the pace."
Europe's Critical Minerals Push
The EC believes that the latest batch of selected projects, combined with the 47 Strategic Projects in the EU and the 13 Strategic Projects in overseas countries that were selected in March and June last year respectively, will make a significant contribution to achieving the EU's CRM derisking and diversification targets. "They could fully meet the extraction benchmarks for lithium, nickel, rare earth elements, magnesium and tungsten, and the processing benchmarks for lithium and rare earth elements," it stated. "They could also cover 89% of the processing benchmark for cobalt and 57% and 51% for tungsten and magnesium respectively, while fully meeting the recycling benchmarks for lithium, cobalt and rare earth elements". Earlier this year, Industrial Info reported that Europe's first complete cycle lithium mining project had completed construction in Syväjärvi in western Finland. Finland will be the first European country to operate a full lithium production cycle, from mining to refining. At full capacity, it will produce roughly 15,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium hydroxide annually at its refinery in Kokkola for at least 18 years - equivalent to around 10% of Europe's current demand.
RESourceEU Action Plan
At the end of last year, the EC launched its RESourceEU Action Plan, similar to the REPowerEU strategy that has greatly helped the bloc cut its reliance on Russian oil and gas. It was given 3 billion euros (US$3.45 billion) for 2026 to support "projects that can provide alternative supplies in the short term." This included immediate financial support for priority projects, such as Vulcan Energy Resources' lithium extraction project in Germany and the Greenland Resources' Malmbjerg molybdenum project in Greenland. Industrial Info is tracking 3 Greenland Resources' projects worth US$870 million in investment, alongside 15 projects related to Vulcan's lithium plans in Germany's Upper Rhine Valley worth more than US$1.8 billion.
Key Takeaways
- The European Commission (EC) has added 46 projects to its rapidly growing list of strategic critical minerals projects.
- By 2030 the EU needs to meet at least 10% of its annual consumption for extraction, 40% for processing and 25% for recycling.
- Industrial Info Resourcesis tracking 11 lithium extraction projects in Europe worth almost US$1.3 billion in investment.

That episode exposed a vulnerability in the supply chain that is easy to miss. While China accounted for 94% of global permanent-magnet production in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), India’s domestic permanent-magnet production capacity remains limited, and imports meet much of its current demand.
But magnets are only one part of a much larger problem.
Also Read | India’s bid to keep carbon cash home as Europe adds a new trade cost
India has significant critical-mineral resources in the ground, but the bottleneck lies in suitable commercial extraction, processing raw ore into refined, high-purity material and then turning those into products such as permanent magnets.
A supply chain built on imports
Ministry of Mines data show that India relied entirely on imports for lithium, cobalt and nickel in FY23, while overseas supplies accounted for about 93% of its copper ore and concentrate needs.
According to a report by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), supplier shares vary by mineral and product category. Finland supplied nearly 60% of India's cobalt oxide and hydroxide imports in FY25. Ireland accounted for close to 40% of lithium carbonate imports, while Chile supplied over 41% of lithium oxide and hydroxide.
Also Read | On Edge: The Great Nicobar project faces a great engineering question
Tanzania accounted for more than half of India's copper ore and concentrate imports, while Chile was the largest supplier across the category, according to IEEFA.
A Press Information Bureau (PIB) release said that between 2022 and 2025, China supplied nearly 60-80% of India's permanent-magnet imports by value and 85-90% by quantity.
India has also sought to diversify its sources. It signed a rare-earths agreement with Brazil in February 2026 and agreed to expand critical-minerals cooperation with Uzbekistan in August 2026. It has also signed mineral agreements with Argentina, Australia and Japan, and explored or pursued cooperation with Germany, Canada, France, the Netherlands, Peru and Chile.
According to a Reuters report, India is also nearing a preliminary pact with Russia on critical minerals.
One supply chain behind a phone, a car and a chip
Rare-earth magnets sit inside an EV’s motor, while its battery relies on minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and graphite. Wind turbines also use magnets, and smartphones use them in small motors and speakers.
Chipmaking, meanwhile, relies on a different set of critical minerals and materials.
India is looking to build capacity across these supply chains. The Union Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0 in July to support chip design and the machines and materials behind manufacturing. The first phase approved 12 manufacturing units, while the second phase expands the programme's focus on the wider semiconductor ecosystem.
According to Singh, GSI is also expanding exploration beyond conventional battery minerals to include elements important for electronics, solar energy, defence and advanced manufacturing.
The riches-and-refineries gap
India’s critical-mineral resource bases are spread across several states.
PIB reported 13.15 million tonnes of monazite containing an estimated 7.23 million tonnes of rare-earth oxides, spread across states from Odisha and Kerala to Gujarat and Jharkhand. It added that the GSI has identified 482.6 million tonnes of rare-earth ore resources across 34 exploration projects.
That figure is ore, not finished rare-earth material, and the difference is the whole story.
Singh cautioned that the approximately 482-million-tonne estimate is largely attributable to beach-sand resources and does not establish how much material is commercially viable or ready for mining.
Grade alone is insufficient to determine a deposit’s potential: mineralogy, mineral associations, liberation characteristics and beneficiation performance also influence how much valuable material can be recovered.
GSI is investigating deposits beyond beach sands, including the Siwana Ring Complex in Rajasthan, which offers potential for heavy rare-earth elements.
“Deloitte’s analysis identifies midstream processing, refining and conversion into high-purity materials as one of the binding constraints in India’s critical-mineral value chain,” Shailesh Tyagi, Partner and Sustainability & Climate Leader at Deloitte South Asia, told ET Online.
He pointed to three gaps.
The first is lithium: India has strong research, but little proven large-scale capacity to make battery-grade lithium carbonate and hydroxide.
The second is rare-earth extraction, refining and magnet production: state-run IREL already runs a rare-earth extraction plant in Odisha and a refining unit at Aluva in Kerala, but Tyagi said the missing link is industrial-scale conversion of separated oxides into metals, alloys and finished magnets.
The third is battery-grade graphite, which he said needs far stricter purity and particle control than mining alone provides.
FICCI Director General Jyoti Vij said India has strong science through CSIR laboratories, BARC and other institutions. The gap is in scaling lab and pilot processes into industrial plants.
She recommended technology partnerships rather than stand-alone imports, including licensing, joint ventures, joint research and pilot-to-commercial projects. Licences should also include process know-how, quality-control protocols and workforce training, she said.
Meanwhile, GSI said it is strengthening the scientific foundation for this transition. The organisation analyses approximately six lakh samples annually, around half associated with critical minerals, and has reduced the turnaround time for exploration reports from 18 months to 15 months.
The government's bet
The centrepiece of this effort is the National Critical Mineral Mission. Its targets include 1,200 domestic exploration projects, self-sufficiency in processing at least five critical minerals, 1,000 patents and four regional processing parks by FY31.
Exploration is also gathering pace. According to Singh, GSI’s critical-mineral exploration programme has grown from around 60 projects in 2020-21 to approximately 300 projects in 2026-27.
GSI also handed over 39 geological memoranda and reports on critical minerals for auction during field season 2025-26, with another 50 blocks targeted for submission by the end of that field season. Singh said close to 40 blocks covering critical minerals, including rare earths, graphite, lithium and cobalt, had been auctioned based on GSI’s geological reports or memoranda.
The Ministry of Mines has further reported that the average time to operationalise a block has fallen from 43 months for FY16-FY21 auctions to 25 months for those since FY22.
However, the magnet push is the most direct answer to the China shock.
A ₹7,280 crore scheme approved in November 2025 aims to build 6,000 tonnes a year of integrated magnet capacity, with ₹6,450 crore in sales-linked incentives and a ₹750 crore capital subsidy. In August 2026, the Ministry of Heavy Industries received 20 bids, and up to five winners, each with an annual capacity of up to 1,200 tonnes, will be chosen. Larsen & Toubro, Coal India and ReNew are among the bidders.
The Union Budget 2026-27 also announced dedicated rare-earth corridors in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
Recycling offers another route to reducing import dependence. A ₹1,500 crore scheme approved in September 2025 aims to build at least 270 kilotonnes of annual recycling capacity, yielding around 40 kilotonnes of critical minerals, with about ₹8,000 crore of investment.
How big is the job, and who pays?
Tyagi said the requirements vary by mineral.
He cited government expectations of 6,000 tonnes a year of magnet capacity, against domestic demand estimates of about 8,220 tonnes a year to 2030. On batteries, he said NITI Aayog's analysis of a 100 GWh scenario implies roughly 56,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate and hydroxide and 98,000 tonnes of graphite by 2030.
The investment required also varies by mineral and processing route.
Tyagi cited estimates of ₹14,400-15,880 crore for neodymium-praseodymium processing and separation in one study, and ₹75,000 crore for graphite refining in another, and said they should not be added together.
His central point is that India needs "bankable" capacity, meaning proven technology, secure feedstock, competitive costs, qualified products and long-term buyers. India needs a few highly utilised plants, he said, rather than hundreds of pilot projects.
Vij argued for layered, mineral-specific support: viability-gap funding, long-tenor loans and credit guarantees at the start, then time-bound production incentives. She also called for long-term purchase commitments from battery, magnet, auto and defence buyers.
“The true measure of mineral security,” Vij said, “is not ownership of ore deposits, but the ability to convert minerals into high-value products domestically.”
India has the resources. The next few years will show whether its refineries can close the crucial gaps.
