articles.title: Copper boom belies a deepening ‘mining recession’ in top producer - Mining.com
articles.summary: Copper boom belies a deepening ‘mining recession’ in top producer  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Chile’s aging copper mines have been battered by deadly accidents, extreme weather and operational missteps, raising questions over how quickly the world’s biggest producer can recover from its lowest output in more than two decades.
At least seven workers have died at Chilean mines in the past month, including two in an avalanche at Codelco’s El Teniente operation. Severe rain and snow have repeatedly disrupted mines and infrastructure, while simmering labor tensions are adding another layer of uncertainty even after workers at an Antofagasta Plc mine ended a strike and BHP Group (ASX: BHP) narrowly averted a walkout at Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine.
The troubles are playing out as traders, producers and investors gather for LME Week in London, where faltering mine supply is likely to be a key topic as participants negotiate contracts for 2027.
While tariff-related trade flows have been the main driver of record copper prices this year, mining problems are another critical factor, particularly in Chile, which accounts for more than 20% of global mined supply. The setbacks are increasing the likelihood of the first annual decline in global mine output since 2017 — just as demand from data centers and power-grid expansion accelerates.
The recent spate of extreme weather is exposing a longer-term dilemma for an industry built around Chile’s historically arid conditions. It also offers a glimpse of what could lie ahead for mines and infrastructure as a powerful El Niño develops. Higher summer temperatures risk causing ice masses to shift at high-altitude operations, threatening pit stability and transport routes.
“There’s clearly a strong influence from climate change and the mining sector’s limited ability to adapt,” said Cristian Cifuentes, head of research at Chilean copper-study center Cesco.
Weather disruptions are landing on top of more fundamental hurdles. Chile’s giant mines are growing older; pits are getting deeper and ore quality is deteriorating, meaning companies have to move and process more material to produce the same amount of copper. Jefferies analysts estimate Chilean open pits experience about a 2% annual natural production decline, with recent investment not enough to offset it.
Chile is in a “major mining recession,” Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz said in September. He expects output to fall about 7% this year before partially recovering in 2027. A decline of that magnitude would put production at roughly 5 million metric tons, the lowest annual level since 2003. Back then, global demand was about 45% lower and Chile accounted for more than a third of the world’s mined copper, just as China’s commodities boom was dawning.
A decade ago, the Chilean state copper commission Cochilco estimated the country had the potential to produce 8.5 million tons by 2025, if projects in the pipeline were realized. Even in 2022, the agency was forecasting 6.4 million tons for 2025. Instead, new projects and expansions have repeatedly failed to offset declining grades and maturing mines.
There’s considerable debate over how bad this year will be and how quickly production can recover. Cochilco forecasts a 2.6% decline this year before a 5.2% rebound in 2027, while consultant CRU Group is set to lower its forecast for a roughly 3% drop to something closer to 5%, analyst Nicolas Muñoz said. CRU expects it will take until 2030 for Chile to return to 6 million tons, given the shortage of large new projects.
“It’s not because we are pessimistic, it’s because we don’t have a technical reason” to expect a faster recovery, Muñoz said.
Codelco lies at the heart of the issue. The state-owned producer is struggling to stabilize output after a yearslong decline amid false starts at projects to overhaul aging mines. Fatal accidents and weather interruptions have plagued its largest mine, while Codelco is investigating potential irregularities in production figures from 2024 and 2025.
The company is changing course under Chairman Bernardo Fontaine, tempering the previous administration’s drive to restore production to historical levels in favor of productivity and profitability. The shift could ultimately mean a smaller workforce as Codelco seeks to contain costs and maximize value from its existing operations.
That points to a two-sided risk for Chilean supply. Codelco’s heavy debt load and strained finances complicate the investments needed to stabilize and grow production. But even cash-rich producers face deteriorating ore quality, extreme weather and increasingly difficult geology.
Output at BHP’s Escondida plunged 28% from a year earlier in August. Production at Collahuasi, owned by Anglo American Plc and Glencore Plc, fell 25%, which a union leader attributed to weather and maintenance among other factors. It hasn’t been all doom and gloom, with Antofagasta reporting growth in the third quarter, albeit slower than analyst expectations.
Labor tensions remain a flashpoint. More than 1,000 supervisors and staff at Escondida accepted a last-minute agreement that averted a strike, while 709 workers at Antofagasta’s Centinela returned to work after a strike lasting more than a week. Codelco is seeking to recover bonuses paid to employees after correcting overstated production figures.
BHP’s Spence mine is suing its workers’ union over stoppages it alleges were illegal. The union described the lawsuit as an intimidation tactic, saying it distorted a dispute rooted in longstanding health and safety concerns.
Jefferies analysts say structural constraints mean increasingly heavy investment will be needed just to maintain output. CRU has turned more optimistic on copper as supply concerns mount, forecasting prices to average about $6.20 a pound in 2027, well above its June outlook. Still, that’s below current levels of around $6.60.
Cesco’s Cifuentes cautions against interpreting this year’s slump as the start of an inexorable decline. He expects Chile to eventually return to growth, albeit too slowly to maintain its share of global production. That will require private projects to materialize, Codelco to execute its structural investments and new technologies to unlock more from existing resources.
“The market will have to get used to a Chile that is stagnant and has a smaller share, rather than a Chile in free fall,” Cifuentes said.
(By James Attwood)

articles.title: Copper shortage pushes mining companies to look for new ways to find metal - 10/12 Industry Report
articles.summary: Copper shortage pushes mining companies to look for new ways to find metal  10/12 Industry Report
articles.full_text:
A looming global copper shortage is pushing mining companies to find new ways to extract more metal from existing mines as demand grows for electric vehicles, power grids, renewable energy and artificial intelligence data centers, Bloomberg reports.
Research firm S&P Global projects the world could face a 10 million-metric-ton copper shortfall by 2040, representing a 25% gap between projected supply and demand. Declining ore quality, high development costs and regulatory hurdles make opening new mines increasingly difficult, prompting companies to explore innovative extraction technologies.
One promising approach is bioleaching, which uses specialized microorganisms to break down surrounding minerals and release copper from ore. Denver-based startup Endolith is testing its technology at Arizona’s Carlota Mine, where customized microbial communities could extend the life of a facility producing roughly one-third of its peak output and facing closure by the end of the decade.
Founded in 2023, Endolith has raised approximately $23 million in venture capital and partnered with mining companies BHP and Rio Tinto to evaluate its technology. The company’s broader goal is to extract at least 10% more copper from low-grade ore, while its work at Carlota could also reduce sulfuric acid consumption.
Advances in DNA sequencing, cloud computing and artificial intelligence have accelerated microbial analysis, but questions remain about whether the technology can perform consistently under unpredictable commercial mining conditions. Endolith’s upcoming field demonstration at Carlota will be a critical test of its effectiveness and scalability, while its economics remain unproven at industrial scale. Even if successful, the company must tailor its microbial solutions to the distinct geological and chemical conditions of individual mines.
As copper demand intensifies, bioleaching could offer an alternative to developing new mines, though its long-term financial and environmental benefits remain to be established.

articles.title: FG Targets 2060 For Solar-Powered Electricity, Green Hydrogen - Majorwaves Energy Report
articles.summary: FG Targets 2060 For Solar-Powered Electricity, Green Hydrogen  Majorwaves Energy Report
articles.full_text:
The Federal Government has set 2060 as its target for developing a power system largely powered by solar energy and storage, with green hydrogen expected to provide backup electricity and reduce carbon emissions from heavy industries.
The Director-General of the Energy Commission of Nigeria, Dr Mustapha Abdullahi, disclosed this at the second International Green Hydrogen Summit held at Afe Babalola University, Ado-Ekiti, on Saturday.
Represented by Bolaji Sulu-Ibrahim, Abdullahi said Nigeria needed to accelerate investment in renewable energy technologies, scientific research and local manufacturing to achieve the target.
Speaking on the theme, “Nigeria’s Pathway to Clean Energy: The Science, Policy and Industry Nexus,” he said the country had substantial renewable energy resources but needed stronger collaboration among government, academia and industry to harness them.
He noted that solar radiation in parts of the North-West, particularly Sokoto, Kebbi and Zamfara states, ranged between 6.0 and 7.0 kilowatt-hours per square metre daily, offering significant opportunities for solar power generation.
According to him, Nigeria also has considerable hydropower resources, wind potential in parts of the North and abundant biomass. However, its installed renewable energy capacity stood at approximately 2,638 megawatts in 2024.
Abdullahi said the disparity between the country’s renewable energy potential and its installed capacity highlighted the need for greater investment in research, technology development and infrastructure.
He disclosed that the commission was implementing a solarisation programme targeting public facilities, particularly those in the health and education sectors. He added that its six energy research centres across the geopolitical zones were expected to strengthen research and innovation.
The commission’s director-general identified dependence on imported solar modules, inverters and batteries, inadequate grid infrastructure, shortages of skilled personnel, substandard equipment and limited access to finance as major challenges facing the sector.
He called for local manufacturing, improved grid integration, stronger quality standards and innovative financing models, stressing that developing the sector required more than laboratory inventions.
On green hydrogen, Abdullahi said electricity accounted for between 60 and 80 per cent of production costs, making affordable renewable energy essential to the technology’s commercial viability.
He added that approximately 1,583 megawatts of underutilised hydropower capacity could complement variable solar generation and support green hydrogen production.
Abdullahi also called for the expedited approval of the draft National Hydrogen Policy, the establishment of a National Hydrogen Council and the development of a national framework for hydrogen research, education and capacity building.
He urged universities and research institutions to collaborate with the commission on research and pilot projects, while encouraging industries to invest in technologies capable of reducing emissions from fertiliser production, refining, cement and steel manufacturing.
The Chief Executive Officer of CrossAfrique Hydrogen Limited, Netherlands, Joshua Dauda, said collaboration among universities, industries and international partners was essential to advancing Nigeria’s clean energy sector.
Dauda disclosed that his company was working with industrial partners and the German development agency, GIZ, to establish a Green Energy Hub at ABUAD.
He said the project would begin with a solar photovoltaic system to power the university and a hydrogen classroom for research and demonstration.
Describing the proposed initiative as potentially the first of its kind in Nigeria, Dauda said it would provide training opportunities for researchers, lecturers and other professionals in hydrogen technology.
He explained that the project would adapt knowledge and expertise gained through international collaboration to Nigeria’s energy needs.
According to him, the initiative would also promote curriculum development and knowledge-sharing, enabling other universities and institutions to replicate the model.
Dauda added that a subsequent phase could explore green ammonia production for fertiliser, potentially extending the project’s benefits to agriculture and industrial development.
Earlier, the Vice-Chancellor of ABUAD, Prof. E. Smaranda Olarinde, called for stronger partnerships among government, academia and industry to translate scientific research into practical clean energy solutions.
Olarinde said Nigeria’s energy transition required sustained investment in research, effective policies, industrial innovation and the development of skilled workers.
She urged participants to ensure that the summit produced practical solutions and lasting partnerships capable of advancing the country’s clean energy ambitions.

Greenzo Energy India today announced that it has secured approximately INR 251 crore ($26.4 million) in cumulative capital across three investment rounds to advance its green hydrogen business. The latest INR 130-crore funding round was led by Ashish Kacholia and his associates, valuing the green-hydrogen platform at around INR 1,030 crore post-money.

Prince Harjai, partner at PARV And Co., acted as the exclusive financial advisor to Greenzo Energy for the transaction.
Greenzo Energy plans to deploy the fresh capital to expand indigenous electrolyser manufacturing capacity, strengthen backward integration, advance research and development, support working capital requirements, and accelerate project execution across domestic and international markets.
“This INR 251-crore total capital raise across rounds, culminating in the latest INR 130-crore funding, reflects strong investor trust in Greenzo’s technology roadmap and execution capabilities,” said Sandeep Agarwal, founder and managing director of Greenzo Energy India. “India’s policy support for green hydrogen is helping lay the foundation for a domestic industry. Our focus is to deploy these funds towards building indigenous manufacturing capabilities, advancing technology and delivering integrated solutions for Indian and international markets.”
Greenzo has a 250 MW-per-annum electrolyser manufacturing facility at Sanand GIDC in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. The facility produces localized alkaline water electrolysers, integrated Balance of Plant (BoP) systems, and provides EPC and O&M services. Greenzo Energy has already executed megawatt-scale green-hydrogen installations for major enterprises, including Engineers India Ltd (EIL), Oswal Energies, and Jindal Stainless Ltd (JSL).

The company has attracted interest from traditional commodity traders and strategic partners seeking domestic copper supplies, CEO Taylor Melvin told Bloomberg News. He declined to identify the prospective buyers but said offtake agreements could include financing to help develop the mine.
“We need a lot more than Santa Cruz to fill that gap,” Melvin said, referring to the widening divide between US copper demand and domestic production.
The negotiations come as copper prices hover near record highs and major technology companies seek to secure supplies for data centres and electricity networks. Global demand growth is expected to outpace production, increasing pressure on the US to develop new mines and reduce its reliance on imported metal.
Financing talks
US President Donald Trump publicly backed financing for Santa Cruz during an Aug. 7 mining roundtable at the State Department, highlighting the project’s importance to efforts to expand domestic mineral production.
That same month, Ivanhoe Electric received a Preliminary Project Letter (PPL) from the Export-Import Bank of the United States (US EXIM) outlining up to $1.1 billion in potential debt financing. The letter represents a preliminary step rather than a final loan commitment.
The company is also discussing project financing with about a dozen commercial banks, Melvin said.
Santa Cruz could become one of the first major new US copper mines in nearly two decades. A preliminary feasibility study released last year estimated initial development costs at $1.24 billion, while the more recent figure for the project’s first phase stands at $1.4 billion. First production is targeted for 2029.
Melvin said the project, combined with nearby resources, could eventually establish one of the country’s leading copper-producing regions.
The financing discussions highlight the capital requirements facing US copper developers as they seek to bring new production online. Potential supply agreements could provide an additional source of funding, although Ivanhoe has yet to announce binding deals.
Technology advantage
Santa Cruz plans to use an on-site processing method that produces copper cathode, a refined form of the metal that can be manufactured into wire, cable and foil. Ivanhoe has promoted the approach as part of its strategy to develop a lower-emissions operation.
The technology could appeal to buyers seeking more direct access to finished copper products while reducing the need for conventional processing facilities.
Major technology companies are already exploring alternative production methods to secure future supplies. Earlier this year, Amazon agreed to purchase copper from Gunnison Copper Corp.’s Arizona mine using proprietary leaching technology developed by Rio Tinto (ASX, LON: RIO).
The process avoids conventional smelting and refining, with the resulting copper destined for Amazon’s data centres.
For Ivanhoe, securing customers and financing will be crucial to advancing Santa Cruz toward its planned 2029 start-up. The project’s development timeline also underscores the challenge facing the global copper industry: demand is accelerating faster than new domestic mines can be brought into production.

Highlights
- Copper traded near record territory, keeping metals and mining names firmly in view.
- The miner detailed brisk latest-quarter copper output across an international portfolio.
- Tight global supply and steady industrial demand continued to underpin the red metal.
Copper took center stage as the trading week began, hovering near record levels after a stretch of steady advances. The red metal has become a barometer for industrial momentum, and its advance kept the spotlight on large diversified miners. The move higher reflected a mix of constrained ore supply, resilient consumption from construction and electrification, and a softer tone in the dollar.
Inside the Latest Production Update
The miner's latest-quarter update pointed to solid copper output drawn from operations spread across several continents. Production figures underscored the scale of the business and its ability to keep metal flowing even as conditions shift across individual sites. Gold volumes, a meaningful byproduct at certain locations, added another layer to the quarterly picture.
A Sprawling Global Mining Footprint
Operations span North and South America alongside a cornerstone presence in Indonesia, giving the company exposure to a range of geologies, cost structures, and regulatory settings. That geographic spread helps smooth the inevitable bumps that come with extracting metal from sole deposits. The diversified base also means the company participates in copper demand wherever it emerges, from grid build-outs to manufacturing hubs.
The Grasberg Complex in Context
Underground development at a deposit of this size is a demanding undertaking, requiring sustained capital and careful sequencing. As the block-cave operations mature, the district has become a steady contributor to group volumes. The complex also illustrates the long lead times that define the industry: assets of this caliber are rare, and bringing them to full stride takes patience, engineering depth, and disciplined execution across many years. Readers following Metals and Mining Stocks can place this update within its wider category.
Copper Demand and the Electrification Wave
Copper sits at the heart of the broad shift toward electrification. The metal threads through power grids, electric vehicles, data centers, renewable generation, and the wiring that connects modern infrastructure. That structural pull on demand has reshaped how the market views red-metal supply over the long run.
Smelting, Refining and Downstream Reach
Beyond extracting ore from the ground, the company participates in smelting and refining, turning concentrate into finished metal. Smelting capacity also matters in a market where processing bottlenecks can shape the flow of refined copper. By managing pieces of this chain directly, the company can respond to shifting treatment charges and logistics.
Gold Output Adds Another Dimension
While copper defines the company, gold is a meaningful companion metal at certain districts, most notably within the Indonesian complex. With gold trading near record highs after an exceptionally strong stretch, byproduct credits from the yellow metal have taken on added weight in the quarterly story. When gold runs hot, it can offset softer patches elsewhere, and when copper leads, the base-metal engine drives results.
Supply Constraints Across the Industry
The copper industry faces a persistent challenge: new, high-quality deposits are increasingly hard to find and even harder to permit and build. Lead times stretch across many years, grades at established operations tend to decline over time, and water, energy, and community factors add complexity to every project. These constraints have become a defining theme for the sector.
Capital Projects and Expansion Plans
Growth in the industry comes through a steady pipeline of brownfield and greenfield work, debottlenecking, and selective development of new ore bodies. The company has outlined expansion efforts aimed at lifting copper volumes over time, including leaching initiatives that squeeze additional metal from material already extracted. Innovative recovery techniques have drawn particular interest, since they can add meaningful tonnes at relatively modest cost by tapping stockpiles that were previously set aside.
Energy, Costs and Operating Discipline
Extracting and processing metal is energy intensive, and the cost of power, fuel, labor, and consumables feeds directly into unit economics. Keeping costs contained is essential when metal prices swing, and operating discipline separates the strongest producers during both upswings and softer stretches. The company has emphasized efficiency across its districts, managing the many inputs that determine the cash cost of each pound of copper.

articles.title: BloombergNEF’S Transition Metals Outlook 2026: Global Metal Supply Shortages Set to Ease, but Copper Faces a $332 Billion Investment Gap - BloombergNEF
articles.summary: BloombergNEF’S Transition Metals Outlook 2026: Global Metal Supply Shortages Set to Ease, but Copper Faces a $332 Billion Investment Gap  BloombergNEF
articles.full_text:
London, October 20, 2026 – Global shortages of metals essential to the energy transition, forecast to emerge across several key commodities a few years ago, are now expected to ease significantly. However, a looming copper deficit could threaten the pace of electrification and require $332 billion of investment in new mines, according to BloombergNEF’s (BNEF) Transition Metals Outlook 2026.
The outlook for metals has improved considerably in recent years. Just a few years ago, the risk of widespread shortages threatened to constrain the shift to cleaner technologies. BNEF now expects nine of the 10 materials covered in its outlook to have sufficient long-term supply capacity through 2050, provided producers continue to develop mines and replace depleted reserves. This marks an improvement on last year’s outlook, when three materials were projected to face deficits.
Copper remains the major exception. BNEF forecasts a supply deficit beginning in 2028 and widening to 20 million metric tons by 2050 – equivalent to 44% of projected global demand. The shortfall could push up prices, force manufacturers to use alternative materials and slow the deployment of electric vehicles, batteries and electricity grids.
Even with the necessary investment, bringing new mines into operation takes an average of 17 years, meaning the shortfall could persist for decades. Declining ore quality and years of underinvestment in exploration are adding to the challenge.
What’s more, demand for copper is expected to rise by 61% between 2026 and 2050, reaching almost 46 million tons. Growing demand from electric vehicles, electricity grids and other applications is putting pressure on supply, with copper use in electrified transport alone projected to increase by 244% to 11.4 million tons
Martin Tengler, Head of Metals and Mining at BloombergNEF, said: “The outlook for transition metals has changed dramatically. Investment in new supply and advances in battery technology have eased many of the concerns we saw just a few years ago. The challenge now is less about whether the world can produce enough metals overall, and more about whether the right materials will be available when and where they are needed. For governments and businesses, securing reliable supply and making the right investment decisions will be increasingly important.”
Other key findings from the report include:
- Lithium demand is forecast to nearly triple to 4.8 million metric tons of lithium carbonate equivalent by 2050 from 1.6 million tons in 2026, while graphite demand is set to more than double to 6.9 million metric tons from 3.3 million. Both jumps are driven by the growth of electric vehicles and energy storage.
- Meanwhile, the growing adoption of lithium iron phosphate batteries has reduced BNEF’s projected demand for cobalt and nickel compared with previous editions of the report.
- China continues to dominate global metals refining, raising supply security concerns. Eight of the 10 materials studied have more than half their refining capacity concentrated in a single country; seven of these are in China.
- Oversupply could put pressure on prices and mining investment. BNEF expects long-term downward price pressure on cobalt, lithium, manganese, nickel and palladium, potentially prompting miners to cut costs, limit production or close capacity. Graphite, platinum and steel have shifted from projected deficits to surpluses compared with last year’s outlook.
- Short-term shortages on some metals remain a risk despite improvements on long-term supply. Lithium faces a temporary deficit, but this is expected to ease as new capacity comes online in 2027. Meanwhile, palladium’s deficit is projected to persist until around 2034. Government restrictions on cobalt exports from the Democratic Republic of Congo and nickel production in Indonesia could also constrain availability.
- Recycling will become essential to meeting global metals demand. Six of the 10 materials studied will require recycling to meet projected demand by 2035, rising to eight by 2050.
BloombergNEF clients can find the full report and full data viewer on bnef.com and the Bloomberg Terminal.
Notes to Editor
The Transition Metals Outlook (TMO) is BloombergNEF’s annual long-term outlook for metals essential to the energy transition. TMO 2026 projects long-term demand, supply capacity, availability and security, and near-term price trends, for 10 metals and minerals: aluminum, cobalt, copper, graphite, lithium, manganese, nickel, platinum, palladium and steel.

articles.title: Singapore LNG Corp. breaks ground on third jetty at Jurong Island terminal to expand small-scale bunkering capacity - Energies Media
articles.summary: Singapore LNG Corp. breaks ground on third jetty at Jurong Island terminal to expand small-scale bunkering capacity  Energies Media
articles.full_text:
Singapore LNG Corp. (SLNG) broke ground on a third jetty at its Jurong Island terminal — the start of what will become the facility’s first berth built exclusively for small- and mid-scale LNG vessels. SLNG Chairman Gan Seow Kee, CEO Leong Wei Hung, and Rotary Engineering Chairman Roger Chia officiated the ceremony together.
Jetty 3 is targeted for completion in the second half of 2028. It’ll handle LNG carriers ranging from 204,825 to 2,825,173 cubic feet (5,800 m³ to 80,000 m³) in capacity — a segment that Singapore, the world’s top LNG bunkering port in 2025, hasn’t had dedicated infrastructure for. Until now.
Groundbreaking ceremony marks start of Jetty 3 construction
The formal groundbreaking brought together leadership from both SLNG and its construction partner. SLNG Chairman Gan Seow Kee and CEO Leong Wei Hung officiated alongside Roger Chia, Chairman of Rotary Engineering Pte. Ltd. — the contractor tapped to build the new berth.
SLNG is building for a market that’s still developing — that carries risk, but it also puts the terminal ahead of demand rather than scrambling to catch up.
Rotary Engineering’s involvement points to a structured, contractor-led build rather than a phased internal expansion. The completion target is set for the second half of 2028, giving the project roughly two and a half years to deliver infrastructure Singapore’s bunkering market is already waiting on.
None of SLNG’s existing jetties are dedicated to small and mid-scale LNG vessels. That gap has become harder to ignore as the bunkering market has grown.
Why SLNG is investing in new jetty infrastructure now
Singapore’s ranking as the world’s top LNG bunkering port in 2025 is a milestone — but it also creates an obligation. Holding that position means building infrastructure that keeps pace with a fast-moving market.
Globally, around 1,700 LNG dual-fuelled vessels are expected to be in operation by 2029. That’s a significant fleet, and each of those ships needs reliable bunkering access. Ports that can’t accommodate the full range of vessel sizes risk losing business to competitors that can.
Jetty 3 directly closes a gap in SLNG’s current vessel-size coverage. By handling LNG carriers from 204,825 to 2,825,173 cubic feet (5,800 m³ to 80,000 m³), the new jetty opens up a segment that existing berths don’t serve on a dedicated basis. That’s not a minor tweak — it’s a structural expansion of what the terminal can offer.
The growing bio-LNG market adds another layer of urgency. Shipping companies looking for lower-carbon fuel options need infrastructure that can handle bio-LNG and verify its sustainability credentials — a combination that’s increasingly a prerequisite for serious market participation.
Capacity and operational scope Jetty 3 will add upon completion
When Jetty 3 comes online in the second half of 2028, it’s expected to support approximately 2 million metric tons per year of LNG bunker reload demand on its own — a substantial addition to what the terminal can process.
Combined with SLNG’s existing infrastructure, the terminal could potentially handle up to 3 million tpy of LNG bunker reload in total, though SLNG notes that figure depends on market demand. It’s a ceiling, not a guarantee. Still, it reflects the scale of ambition behind the investment.
Beyond bunkering, Jetty 3 will also accommodate break-bulk and other small-scale LNG operations. Not every terminal customer is a large shipping company fueling a container vessel — smaller distributors and regional operators need access too, and the new berth is designed with them in mind. It’ll also be capable of handling bio-LNG, tying its physical infrastructure directly to SLNG’s broader sustainability positioning as the fuel mix in maritime shipping continues to shift.
SLNG Terminal receives ISCC EU certification for bio-LNG handling
Physical capacity alone isn’t enough to compete in the bio-LNG market. Customers need assurance that the fuel they’re purchasing has been properly tracked and verified — and that’s where certification becomes decisive.
The SLNG Terminal is among the first in the region to obtain ISCC EU certification for bio-LNG handling — a meaningful distinction in a market where trust in sustainability claims is still being established. The certification covers storage, regasification and send-out, bunkering, and trucking. Across all of these services, the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification EU framework verifies that bio-LNG can be traced and accounted for, giving customers documented confidence in what they’re buying.
SLNG is also working with partners to share best practices in bio-LNG certification across the upstream-to-terminal value chain — aimed at strengthening end-user confidence and supporting broader market adoption, not just at the SLNG Terminal but across the ecosystem it operates within.
What the third jetty means for Singapore’s LNG position
The Jetty 3 groundbreaking and the ISCC EU certification together represent a two-track expansion strategy: more physical capacity and stronger sustainability credentials, arriving in parallel. SLNG is building for a market that’s still developing — that carries risk, but it also puts the terminal ahead of demand rather than scrambling to catch up.
The second-half 2028 completion target gives the project a clear timeline. Between now and then, the global LNG dual-fuel fleet will keep growing, bio-LNG adoption will likely accelerate, and Singapore’s role as a bunkering hub will face ongoing pressure to deliver. Jetty 3, once complete, is designed to help the terminal meet those challenges head-on.

articles.title: Middle East LNG industry remains hostage of Iran war - Awani International
articles.summary: Middle East LNG industry remains hostage of Iran war  Awani International
articles.full_text:
AI Brief
- Qatar’s LNG exports remain severely disrupted due to the ongoing Iran war, with export volumes far below pre-war levels and significant damage to infrastructure.
- The disruption has caused global LNG market strain, leading to soaring prices in Asia and Europe and a projected 8.6% contraction in Qatar’s GDP for 2026.
- Despite some recovery in Middle Eastern oil exports, LNG shipments face complex logistical challenges and uncertainty until the Strait of Hormuz is securely reopened.
LONDON: While Middle Eastern oil exports have rebounded in recent weeks, Qatar's vast liquefied natural gas export facilities remain hobbled. Until a durable resolution of the US-Israeli war with Iran is reached, Gulf shipments will be heavily curtailed, leaving the global LNG market seriously strained.
Qatar is the world's second-largest producer of LNG behind the United States. It accounts for around a fifth of global capacity at nearly 80 million metric tons per year.
The Iran war, now in its eighth month, has dealt a heavy blow to Qatar. The country was forced to shut down much of its main LNG complex at Ras Laffan shortly after the start of hostilities and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian missile attacks also knocked out around 17% of Qatar’s export capacity, costing the country tens of billions of dollars in lost annual revenue and inflicting damage that could take years to repair.
The economic blow has been among the biggest in the region. The International Monetary Fund forecasts Qatar’s gross domestic product will contract by 8.6% in 2026, compared with pre-war expectations for 6.1% growth.
The severe disruption to Qatar's LNG exports, alongside a drop in exports from neighbouring United Arab Emirates, has sent shockwaves through global gas markets. The supply hit was partially cushioned by a sharp increase in US exports, which rose by around 14% in 2026 from a year earlier to 123 million tons — but the gap in the global LNG market remained large.
The impact was felt most acutely in Asia and Europe, which rely heavily on LNG imports and have limited alternatives to replace disrupted Gulf supplies. Asian and European LNG prices hit their highest level since early 2023 in late September, nearly tripling from pre-Iran war levels.
While QatarEnergy, the country's national energy company, has indicated it will be able to restart LNG production within weeks once Hormuz reopens, LNG importers should not get too optimistic. A deeper look at Qatar’s current situation suggests its LNG industry won’t be returning to pre-war norms any time soon.
NOT GOOD ENOUGH FOR LNG
The outlook for Gulf crude exports certainly has improved. Iran's grip on Hormuz appears to have weakened in recent weeks, allowing a sharp increase in oil exports from the region.
Middle East crude shipments through Hormuz rose in September to around 80% of pre-war levels at 16 million barrels per day, according to data analytics firm Kpler. Producers appear increasingly confident transiting the waterway with US Navy support, even as Iran’s strikes on shipping have risen in recent weeks to the highest number since the war began.
The increase in exports has allowed Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait and Iraq to raise domestic production meaningfully.
Yet LNG traffic in the Gulf has barely recovered.
While Qatar’s LNG exports rose in September to their highest level since the start of the conflict at 1.6 million tons, that was still less than a quarter of the pre-war average, according to Kpler.
Importantly, around a third of September's exports went to Kuwait, meaning they stayed inside the Gulf. The remaining volumes went to China, India and other Asian countries, with tankers typically switching off their satellite navigation systems when crossing Hormuz.
The outlook isn’t improving. Qatar’s October LNG exports are on track to fall sharply to just 0.6 million tons, according to Kpler, probably as a result of the rise in attacks on ships. And last month QatarEnergy extended force majeure notices, signalling that it remains unable to deliver LNG cargoes to many customers in Asia and Europe.
COMPLEX LOGISTICS
The contrast between the recovery in oil exports and stagnant LNG exports reflects fundamental differences in how the two industries operate.
Oil systems are flexible. They can restart relatively quickly and benefit from extensive storage and shipping logistics. LNG supply chains, on the other hand, are highly integrated, capital intensive and far less tolerant of disruption.
Qatar's LNG facilities consist of 14 production units — known as trains — supplied by gas from the offshore North Field, the world's largest gas reservoir, which the country shares with Iran.
North Field production has been running at minimal rates since the start of the war, just enough to meet Qatar's domestic needs and maintain limited exports.
Restarting the system is not simply a matter of reopening a terminal or dispatching a few tankers.
To increase LNG exports, Qatar would first need to raise gas production. And that is where the logistical challenges become quite complex.
The raw gas extracted from the North Field contains large volumes of very light oil known as condensate, which must be separated and exported. If condensate cannot be shipped out reliably, Qatar risks quickly running out of storage. It could then be forced to curb gas production regardless of LNG demand.
Similarly, Qatar has limited capacity to store LNG itself in onshore tanks or aboard vessels at sea, leaving little room for operational delays if exports are interrupted.
Finally, the global LNG tanker fleet is far smaller than the oil tanker fleet. Freight rates are therefore much higher, while shippers are far less willing to send expensive LNG carriers through Hormuz if there is any risk they could become trapped inside the Gulf for weeks or, worse, get hit by an Iranian strike.
Qatar therefore needs more than occasional safe passage through Hormuz. It needs assurance that all ships will be able to transit the waterway safely.
STRANDED ASSETS
The timing is particularly unfortunate because Qatar is in the middle of a massive expansion programme that will see it raise LNG capacity to 142 million tons per year by 2030. That would give it roughly a quarter of the global market.
But new capacity is of little value if the export route remains uncertain.
Until the strait's security is governed by a credible and durable agreement involving Iran, the United States and regional powers, the world's largest LNG expansion project may remain stranded.
In the meantime, the global LNG market has little hope of a speedy recovery.
The opinions expressed here are those of Ron Bousso, a columnist for Reuters.

The study identified core economic activity and energy source transitions as the largest reasons for additional demand, while AI data centers and defense represent emerging demand drivers.
Supply growth remains a consideration as demand expands. In a separate January 2026 report, S&P Global argued that, without significant additions to global supply, the copper market could face a shortfall of approximately 10 million metric tons by 2040. The study projects that mined copper production could peak around 2030 before declining as existing mines age, while recycled copper would cover only part of the additional demand. The International Energy Agency also continues to track copper as a critical mineral, with its 2026 Critical Minerals Data Explorer providing updated projections for copper demand under multiple energy and technology scenarios.
U.S. trade policy has also affected copper markets and inventories. On April 2, 2026, the White House modified the Section 232 tariff regime for copper, among other metals, so that applicable duties would generally be assessed on the full customs value of covered products rather than only their metal content. The proclamation established additional duties ranging from 10% to 50%, depending on the product, its origin, and its treatment under the applicable provisions.
The tariff changes have contributed to unusual flows of copper into the United States. Reuters reported in August 2026 that U.S. copper imports had reached 885,000 metric tons during the first half of 2026, while COMEX inventories had climbed to a record 675,185 tons as traders responded to the prospect of future tariffs on refined copper. At the same time, copper prices on the London Metal Exchange approached record levels, illustrating how U.S. tariff expectations have affected the distribution of available metal even as the broader global market remained sensitive to supply disruptions and demand growth.
U.S. copper supply remains an important consideration for the domestic market. The U.S. Geological Survey's 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries estimated U.S. mine production at approximately 1 million metric tons in 2025, down from 1.05 million metric tons in 2024, while refined copper production was estimated at 850,000 metric tons. The USGS also added copper to the U.S. critical minerals list in 2025.

articles.title: FERC’s Plan to Speed Up LNG Approvals Must Not Sacrifice Safeguards - Construction Review
articles.summary: FERC’s Plan to Speed Up LNG Approvals Must Not Sacrifice Safeguards  Construction Review
articles.full_text:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has proposed the first blanket authorization program for liquefied natural gas facilities, allowing some LNG projects to proceed without separate, case-specific FERC approval orders. Announced on October 15 in Washington, D.C., the proposal would create a three-tier approval system for LNG terminals and plants across the United States. It promises faster construction and greater regulatory certainty—but only if speed does not weaken environmental review, public participation, and safety oversight.
FERC’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking would let eligible activities at LNG facilities move forward without individual authorization orders under Sections 3 and 7 of the Natural Gas Act. The commission says the program is modeled on its 40-year-old blanket certificate system for interstate natural gas pipelines, which allows routine pipeline work to proceed through notice-based procedures rather than full case-by-case review.
The proposal comes as the United States remains the world’s largest LNG exporter and as developers and policymakers press for faster infrastructure approvals. FERC Chairman Laura V. Swett argues that consumers benefit when energy infrastructure is dependable and affordable, and that essential projects should not face unnecessary delay.
A tiered system, not a blank cheque
The proposal is not a blanket approval for every LNG project. Routine activities that do not increase a plant’s authorized capacity, expand its footprint, or push operations beyond design limits could proceed automatically. Activities that may increase capacity but remain within the existing plant footprint would require 60 days’ prior notice. New liquefaction trains, LNG tanks, marine berths, and related systems—including some work outside an existing plant footprint—would require 90 days’ notice.
That structure is sensible. Replacing equipment or carrying out a safety upgrade is not the same as building a new export terminal or expanding into new land or waterways. Permitting should be proportionate: low-risk work should not wait behind the same process as major construction.
FERC also proposes environmental and engineering conditions, compliance requirements, and coordination with federal and state authorities. For certain LNG terminals, those requirements could involve the U.S. Coast Guard, state agencies, and local emergency-response organizations.
The risk: speed without accountability
But the proposal raises a serious question: faster than what, and at what cost?
Environmental organizations warn that the program could allow projects to receive automatic or expedited approval without full environmental review or adequate oversight. The Sierra Club argues that it could permit methane gas projects to advance without enough scrutiny of local and regional air-quality impacts.
Those concerns cannot be dismissed as routine opposition to natural gas. LNG facilities handle hazardous materials, often operate near communities and waterways, and can affect air quality, traffic, emergency planning, and ecosystems. A process that makes approval easier must not make it harder for residents, states, and local responders to identify risks before construction begins.
The 90-day category deserves particular attention. New tanks, marine berths, and liquefaction trains are not minor modifications. Even FERC’s proposed limits—such as restricting certain expansions to no more than 25 acres of previously disturbed or developed land or waterways—cannot capture every local impact.
Public input must remain real
FERC says prior-notice projects would receive project-specific environmental analysis under the National Environmental Policy Act or qualify for a categorical exclusion. Categorical exclusions may be appropriate for genuinely minor activities, but they become problematic if applied too broadly to projects with meaningful local consequences.
The commission has opened a 60-day comment period after publication in the Federal Register. That period should be more than a legal formality. Developers, states, environmental groups, community organizations, and emergency responders should press FERC on who can protest a project, how communities will be notified, and what evidence will determine whether a project avoids fuller review.
The Constitution Pipeline Project shows why balance matters. FERC approved the Pennsylvania-to-New York natural gas pipeline in 2014, but it stalled for years after New York denied a key water-quality certification. Now, with the Department of Energy pledging up to $42 million to help revive it, the project underscores a broader concern: FERC’s push to accelerate gas infrastructure approvals should speed routine work without weakening the environmental and community reviews that determine whether major projects can proceed responsibly.
The bottom line
America needs to build and maintain energy infrastructure more efficiently. But regulatory certainty should mean developers know the rules—not that communities discover the consequences after decisions are made.
FERC’s LNG blanket authorization proposal could be a major improvement in U.S. energy permitting. It could also become a cautionary tale about confusing speed with progress. FERC should accelerate routine work, but preserve rigorous review where the stakes are highest.

Few metals names carry a footprint as broad as this one. That geographic spread helps smooth the inevitable bumps that come with extracting metal from single deposits.
The diversified base also means the company participates in copper demand wherever it emerges, from grid build-outs to manufacturing hubs. Each district brings its own mix of ore grades and logistics, and the ability to coordinate across them is central to how the business maintains steady metal delivery.
For the metals and mining sector, the breadth of this portfolio makes the company a useful proxy for the health of the copper market as a whole. When a producer operates across so many jurisdictions, its disclosures capture trends in labor, energy, and permitting that reach well beyond any single region, turning each quarterly update into a broad read on the state of global copper supply.

The Grasberg district in Indonesia remains one of the most significant copper and gold complexes anywhere in the world. The downstream footprint rounds out a model that starts at the rock face and extends toward the cathode and rod that industrial customers ultimately use, keeping the business engaged across multiple stages of the copper journey. Market Overview
Green ammonia is produced using hydrogen generated from water electrolysis powered by renewable electricity, followed by conventional ammonia synthesis. It can serve fertilizer and chemical demand without changing the basic molecule, but production costs and emissions depend on the power supply and plant operation.
Early commercial output is concentrated in China and a small number of European plants. Indian supply contracts and international offtake agreements are expanding the project pipeline. GCL and Jurong agree on construction and gas-processing arrangements for the Ogaden Basin project as Ethiopia advances plans to commercialise its natural gas resources and develop international export channels.
Two Chinese companies have signed a construction and processing agreement for the second phase of Ethiopia’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in the Ogaden Basin, advancing plans to expand gas production and develop export markets from the country’s eastern Somali Region.
GCL Group, through its Ethiopian subsidiary, and Jurong Group (Holding) signed the agreement on October 16, 2026, at the Ministry of Mines in Addis Ababa, in the presence of Minister Alemtsehay Paulos.
The contract covers engineering and construction activities as well as contracted natural gas liquefaction and processing services associated with the project’s second phase at the Calub gas field.
The agreement follows the commissioning of the first phase in October 2025 and a strategic cooperation framework signed between the two companies in May 2026.
While the earlier agreement established the partnership, the latest contract sets out more specific responsibilities for constructing liquefaction facilities and providing processing services.
Ethiopia’s Ministry of Mines called for construction of the first module of the second phase to begin as soon as possible, according to the announcement.
However, the companies have not disclosed the contract’s financial value, the additional production capacity, the financing structure or a completion deadline.
The contract was signed by Fu Zhidong, Executive President of GCL’s Ethiopia liquefaction and refining division, and Yi Min, Vice President of Jurong Group.
Lin Rongsheng, Chairman of Jurong Group, said the company would contribute its experience in liquefaction infrastructure, project management, storage, transportation and international trade.
The two companies also intend to cooperate on supporting infrastructure and logistics systems required to transport LNG to domestic and overseas customers.
The project is centred on the Calub gas field, one of Ethiopia’s established natural gas deposits in the Ogaden Basin.
GCL commissioned its first modular LNG facility at Calub on October 2, 2025, with a designed processing capacity of 200,000 cubic metres of natural gas per day and annual LNG production capacity of approximately 50,000 metric tonnes.
The first phase was developed primarily to supply industrial parks and other domestic consumers, while the second phase is intended to increase production and extend sales to international markets.
The project forms part of Ethiopia’s wider effort to develop its petroleum and natural gas resources for industrial use, electricity generation and export earnings.
Despite having identified natural gas resources in the Ogaden Basin decades ago, Ethiopia has historically relied heavily on imported petroleum products to meet commercial and industrial energy demand.
Development of the Calub and Hilala resources has involved successive investment agreements, technical studies and changes in project implementation arrangements.
Commercialisation has depended on the construction of processing facilities, transport infrastructure and systems capable of delivering gas to industrial consumers or international buyers.
The first phase of the LNG project represented an operational step towards domestic gas processing, although its designed production capacity is considerably smaller than the scale envisaged under the broader Ogaden Basin development programme.

articles.title: China in the global lithium-ion battery value chain - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: China in the global lithium-ion battery value chain  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Lithium-ion batteries have become the backbone of the global energy transition. From electric vehicles and renewable energy storage systems to consumer electronics, this technology determines the rate of emission reduction and the level of energy security for many countries. In this complex value chain, spanning from mineral extraction and chemical refining to the production of cathode materials, battery cell assembly, and packaging, China currently holds a near-total dominant position.
According to estimates from the International Energy Agency (IEA), the independent price reporting agency and leading global data provider Benchmark Mineral Intelligence (BMI), and analysis by BloombergNEF, a strategic research organization specializing in global commodity markets and the energy transition, by 2025-2026, China will control approximately 75-80% of global battery cell production capacity, over 85% of cathode materials, over 90% of anode materials, and a similar proportion of electrolytes. Even in lithium refining, where raw materials mainly come from Australia, Chile, and several other countries, China still accounts for 60-75% of the capacity to convert lithium into battery-grade chemicals.
According to the Financial Times , the lithium-ion battery value chain can be divided into three main tiers. At the top tier, China is not the world's largest lithium producer (Australia and Chile lead in mining output), but it dominates the processing stage. Much of Australia's spodumene ore is exported to China for refining into lithium carbonate (a crucial raw material widely used in manufacturing) or lithium hydroxide for battery production. According to BMI data and industry reports, China controls 60-70% of global lithium chemical refining capacity, creating a strategic "bottleneck" advantage.
The next tier is where China's advantage is most evident. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) anode materials are almost exclusively produced by Chinese manufacturers, with global market shares exceeding 95-98% in some segments. Artificial and natural graphite cathode materials, electrolytes, and diaphragms are also heavily concentrated here. Companies such as Hunan Yuneng (LFP anodes), BTR (cathode), Tianci Material (electrolytes), and SEMCORP (diaphragms) have maintained global leadership positions for many consecutive years.
The final tier (including cell and battery pack manufacturing) is dominated by Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Ltd. (CATL – the world's largest electric vehicle battery and energy storage system manufacturer from China) and the new energy vehicle technology and manufacturing conglomerate BYD. According to data from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance (CABIA) and SNE Research, in 2025, CATL is expected to account for approximately 39-43% of the global electric vehicle battery installation market share and maintain its number one position in the domestic Chinese market, with a share of around 41-46% depending on the month in 2026. BYD will rank second with approximately 16-21%. The combined market share of Chinese manufacturers is projected to reach 65-75%, depending on the calculation method.
Sources of competitive advantage
China's advantage doesn't stem from a single factor. First , there's scale. Global lithium-ion battery production capacity is estimated to exceed 4 TWh by the end of 2025, with approximately 80% located in China. This large scale allows for reduced fixed costs, optimized supply chains, and accelerated technology innovation lifecycles. Second , there's cost. Battery pack prices in China are significantly lower than in Europe and North America, potentially by 20-30% or more, according to IEA analyses. Low industrial electricity prices, labor costs, and a dense supplier ecosystem contribute to this gap.
You may also like
Thirdly , there is vertical integration and policy support. Many Chinese enterprises are expanding from mining and importing materials to manufacturing battery cells and vice versa, while investing in mining both domestically and internationally. The Chinese government plays a guiding role through industrial planning, credit support, and policies encouraging electric vehicles and energy storage. By 2026, the Chinese electric vehicle market will account for a very high proportion of new car sales, creating a stable output for the battery industry.
According to the Straits Times, 2025 and the first half of 2026 will see a boom in energy storage batteries alongside electric vehicle batteries. CATL and its competitors are rapidly shifting their focus, with the storage segment becoming a new growth driver. China's battery exports are increasing sharply, especially to Europe, Australia, and several emerging markets.
However, excessive growth led to overcapacity. The industry's average capacity utilization rate fell to low levels, and the prices of anode materials and battery cells plummeted during 2024-2025. By mid-2026, the Chinese government had temporarily halted the approval of new battery plant projects that had not yet commenced construction, aiming to control overcapacity and promote the consolidation of the new energy sector. This move is expected to benefit businesses with high capacity utilization rates, such as CATL.
LFP chemistry (lithium-ion battery technology using lithium iron phosphate compound LiFePO₄ as the anode material) continues to expand its domestic market share, accounting for over 85% of battery installations in China in some months of 2026, thanks to its low cost, high safety, and suitability for mid-range electric vehicles as well as large-scale storage.
Risks and diversification efforts
The high concentration of supply chains poses significant geopolitical and supply security risks. The IEA has repeatedly warned that the majority of batteries used for the grid and over 70% of electric vehicles manufactured outside of China still depend on at least one stage of production in China. Export controls on battery components and technology implemented by Beijing from 2023-2025 further heighten these concerns.
The United States, the European Union (EU), Canada, Australia, and several other countries are investing tens of billions of dollars to build their own supply chains, from lithium refining to the production of battery materials and cells. However, experts believe that bridging the gap will take years and require enormous capital. Production costs outside of China remain significantly higher, while the lack of a complete supplier ecosystem makes scaling up difficult. Some projects have been delayed or canceled as support policies have changed. The chief commercial officer of the specialty chemicals company Albemarle (US) once commented that the difference in processing costs outside of China can be two to three times, making pure price competition very difficult without long-term policy support.
Technology experts predict that China is likely to maintain its leading position in the lithium-ion battery value chain at least until the end of this decade. Its advantages in scale, cost, and a robust ecosystem that is unlikely to erode in the short term continue to hold the advantage for the country with the world's largest population. At the same time, Beijing is also adjusting to reduce domestic overcapacity and improve the quality of growth, focusing on higher energy density technologies and new solid-state batteries.
You may also like
For the world, reliance on a single manufacturing hub presents both opportunities and risks. The opportunity lies in the rapidly falling price of batteries, supporting the deployment of electric vehicles and renewable energy at lower costs. The risk lies in the potential for supply disruptions due to trade tensions, export controls, or geopolitical events.
Experts from the IEA and BloombergNEF agree that diversifying the battery supply chain is necessary, but it must be based on a solid economic foundation, not just state subsidies. Building refining and manufacturing capabilities outside of China will determine the success of this strategy.
In the context of accelerating global energy transition, China's position in the lithium-ion battery value chain is not just an industrial story, but a strategic factor shaping the energy and technology landscape of the next decade. Finding a balance between competition, cooperation, and minimizing concentration risks will directly impact the speed and sustainability of global decarbonization.

Highlights
- Coyote Copper expects drilling at Copper Springs to begin in November.
- Nearly all accelerated warrants were exercised before the deadline.
- Geophysics and sampling results are expected ahead of the drill program.
Copper exploration in the American Southwest continues to draw attention as demand for the metal grows across electrification, power grids and construction. Coyote Copper Mines Inc. (TSXV:CCMM) Basic Materials Coyote Copper Mines Inc. (TSXV:CCMM) 0.45 CAD -0.040 8.247% Last Updated at: 2026-10-19T18:36:00Z , a junior explorer advancing its wholly owned Copper Springs Project in Arizonas Copper Triangle, said it has signed a drilling contract and expects its first drill program to start in the first half of November. Listed on the junior exchange and tracked within the TSX Venture Composite Index, the company is one of the Penny Stocks moving from surface work toward its first meaningful test of a large copper target.
How did the warrant acceleration turn out?
The same release confirmed the outcome of a warrant acceleration the company triggered in mid-September after receiving its first-phase drill permits. Under the warrant terms, receipt of those permits allowed Coyote Copper to accelerate the expiry of certain warrants, giving warrant owners a limited window to exercise or see them expire.
By the deadline in mid-October, nearly all of the accelerated warrants, including finders warrants from earlier financings, had been exercised. The exercise brought in fresh cash without the need for a new financing round. The company said the proceeds will support its ongoing and planned exploration work and the staking and acquisition of additional mining claims.
High exercise rates on accelerated warrants are often read as a sign of engagement from existing shareholders, since they choose to put more money into the company rather than let the warrants lapse.
Where Is Copper Springs?
Copper Springs sits in the Arizona Copper Triangle, a region that has hosted some of North Americas most important copper mines for generations. The project lies just south of Capstone Coppers Pinto Valley Mine, a long-running open-pit operation.
Coyote Copper recently expanded its land position by staking additional claims, building a larger package around its key targets. Being close to established mines brings practical benefits, including nearby infrastructure, roads and a regional workforce familiar with mining.
What is the company targeting?
According to earlier disclosures, geophysical work at Copper Springs has outlined a large subsurface anomaly that Coyote Copper interprets as an intrusive-hydrothermal centre consistent with a porphyry copper system. Soil and bedrock sampling has returned elevated copper values at surface.
The first phase of drilling is designed to test both shallow oxide copper targets and deeper sulphide targets. The company has compared the projects setting with other deposits in the Copper Triangle, which are typically large, lower-grade porphyry systems mined at scale.
Why Porphyry Systems Draw Interest
Porphyry deposits supply most of the worlds copper. They tend to be very large, with mineralization spread through big volumes of rock. While grades are usually modest, their size can support long-life, high-tonnage mining operations.
Arizona is home to many of these systems, which is why explorers continue to look for new ones in the state. Finding a porphyry system is only the start, however. Drilling is needed to determine whether copper is present in sufficient grade and volume, and many targets do not progress beyond early testing.
How do oxide and sulphide targets differ?
Oxide copper ores form near surface where weathering has altered the original minerals. They can often be processed through leaching and solvent extraction methods. Sulphide ores lie deeper and typically require conventional milling and flotation. Testing both gives Coyote Copper a fuller picture of what Copper Springs might contain at different depths.
Why accelerate warrants at all?
Warrant acceleration clauses are a common feature of junior financings. They allow a company to shorten the life of outstanding warrants once a defined milestone is met, such as receiving permits or reaching a trading threshold. For the company, the main benefit is timing: cash arrives when it is most useful, in this case just before a drill program. For warrant owners, the clause creates a clear decision point, since unexercised warrants expire at the deadline. In Coyote Coppers case, the permit milestone that triggered the acceleration was the same one that cleared the path to drilling, linking the funding directly to the work it is meant to support.
The Bigger Picture for Copper Explorers
Copper has become a focal point for the resource sector as governments and industries push toward electrification. Electric vehicles, renewable energy installations and grid upgrades all require significant amounts of the metal. At the same time, new large deposits have become harder to find, and development timelines for new mines are long.
That combination has kept attention on juniors exploring in proven districts. Readers who follow Metal & Mining Stocks will recognize Arizona as one of the jurisdictions where junior explorers continue to test fresh ground near operating mines.
Coyote Copper is moving from preparation to execution at Copper Springs. A signed drilling contract, permits in hand, site preparation underway and fresh funds from its warrant acceleration put the company in position to begin its first drill program in November.
Exploration remains an uncertain process, and the drill bit will be the ultimate test of the porphyry concept the company has outlined. Still, the steps taken over recent weeks give Coyote Copper a clear path toward its next set of results in Arizonas Copper Triangle.

Texas Plant to Extract Lithium from Oil Wastewater
Industrial Info Resources is tracking 55 active lithium mining projects in the U.S. with a total investment value of more than US$41 billion
Released Monday, October 19, 2026
Written by Paul Wiseman for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)
Summary
Various DOE programs help Element3 commercialize revolutionary system for extracting lithium from produced water in Permian Basin.
First Commercial Lithium from Oilfield Produced Water
Output from one plant in Midland, Texas, which started up in February of this year, could match about half of the U.S.'s lithium mining capacity when fully operational.
Except it's not a lithium mine in the traditional sense; instead, it uses a process called direct lithium extraction (DLE) to remove battery-grade lithium powder from water co-produced with oil in oil wells.
Oil wells produce much more water than oil, in ratios of anywhere from 4-1 to 10-1. This "produced water" is rich in salts and minerals, including lithium, that heretofore have simply been pumped as waste into disposal wells.
While efforts to economically extract minerals from produced water have multiplied in the last five to 10 years, Element3's Permian Basin Lithium Extraction and Carbonate facility is among the first to operate on a significant scale.
Industrial Info Resources is tracking 55 active lithium mining projects in the U.S. with TIV of $41.62 billion. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on these projects in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Metals & Minerals Project Database, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in a list of project reports.
How It Works
For this plant, Element3 in 2024 licensed an extraction technology (actually a litany of seven technologies) developed by the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), through the DOE's Critical Materials Innovation Hub.
Said technologies include membrane-extraction techniques and new separation methods that separate lithium chloride from both other elements and the water that contains them. It then converts the lithium chloride into battery-grade lithium carbonate powder.
The final product is a solid, the company reports, which is the main material for the battery supply chain.
Hood Whitson, the founder and chief executive officer of Element3, said in a May 1 interview that the company intends to fill up this plant and expand elsewhere," indicating that the plant is not yet operating at capacity.
U.S. Lithium Needs to Ramp Up
The need for more domestic production is critical, as the U.S. currently produces less than 1% of the world's total lithium, somewhere between 610 and 4,000 tonnes per year. It imports more than half its lithium, mostly from Argentina and Chile, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).
Currently there is only one significant lithium mine, Albemarle's Silverpeak Lithium Solution Mine in Nevada. Subscribers can learn more from a detailed plant profile.
Industrial Info Resources is tracking five active lithium mines, in addition to the 55 projects. If Element3 and other produced water extraction pilot projects take off, this could open new doors to a domestic lithium supply. Significant investment in plants and infrastructure would have to follow, so it could still be years off.
Lithium's U.S. Future Seems Bright
Much has also been invested in DLE extraction from brine in the Smackover Formation that straddles the Arkansas-Texas border. According to the USGS, this could contain anywhere from 5 million to 19 million metric tons of lithium. The wide variance there is because, said the USGS, they only determined lithium's presence, not differentiating based on economic or technical recoverability.
Traditional lithium mining could also be about to explode. The USGS has reported the discovery of significant lithium deposits in two U.S. regions. Last May it said the Appalachian region is estimated to contain 2.3 million metric tons of untapped, economically recoverable lithium. That would replace 328 years of U.S. imports at 2025's rate.
Also, there could be 20 million to 40 million metric tons of lithium-rich clay in the McDermitt Caldera on the Nevada-Oregon border. The USGS says this may be single largest lithium deposit ever found.
Demand Growth Through the Roof
As demand grows from battery electric-storage systems (BESS) to help wind and solar supply baseline power, from EVs and others, supply will have to scramble to keep up, according to many in the industry, including Lithium Harvest.
Lithium Harvest sees demand increasing by three times by 2030 and 4.2 times by 2035. it notes 30% demand growth in 2024 over 2023. EVs and BESS account for more than 60% of lithium use and could reach 90% by 2040.
Key Takeaways
- To meet U.S. and world lithium demands for batteries in EV and BESS systems, it will be all hands on deck for miners.
- Accessing lithium from oilfield produced water, after years of research, is now a viable addition to the mining mix.

articles.title: In 1975, Kodak began operating a uranium-based research device beneath its Rochester laboratory; 31 years - The Times of India
articles.summary: In 1975, Kodak began operating a uranium-based research device beneath its Rochester laboratory; 31 years  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
For most people, Kodak is a name associated with cameras and photographic film. But for 31 years, the American company had something far less familiar inside its research facility in Rochester, New York: a nuclear device containing highly enriched uranium.
The machine began operating in 1975 and remained in use until 2006. Its existence attracted widespread attention only in 2012, years after it had shut down. Now, a report by Popular Mechanics, published on Wednesday, has revisited the unusual facility and explained why the equipment, despite using uranium, was not a self-sustaining nuclear reactor.
The machine was about the size of a refrigerator and was kept in a secure underground laboratory. According to the report, it was not being used to produce electricity or develop nuclear weapons. Kodak's scientists, however, used it to examine materials, identify unwanted substances in chemicals, and look inside objects without damaging them.
The equipment was known as a californium neutron flux multiplier, or CFX, whose purpose was to produce a supply of neutrons, tiny particles found inside atoms, which scientists could use to study different materials.
What later drew attention was the uranium inside the machine. Highly enriched uranium can also be used in nuclear weapons, raising questions about why a photography company had access to it. However, the device had operated under government supervision, and its existence had been mentioned in scientific papers even though Kodak had not widely publicised it.
Why did Kodak need nuclear equipment?
Kodak's work involved more than making cameras and selling photographic film. The company also carried out research into the materials and chemicals used in its products. Scientists needed to check what those materials contained and whether unwanted substances were present.
The nuclear device helped them do this in two ways. The first was a process called neutron activation analysis. Scientists directed neutrons at a sample, causing some of its atoms to release signals in the form of gamma rays. By measuring those signals, researchers could identify the elements present in the material. This allowed them to detect impurities.
The second method, neutron radiography, helped scientists examine the inside of an object without cutting it open.This makes neutron imaging useful for examining certain lighter materials, including water and photographic film, that may not show up clearly in ordinary X-ray images.
Why was Kodak's machine different from a nuclear reactor?
The machine used two radioactive materials to produce the neutrons needed for its experiments. One was californium-252, a substance that naturally releases neutrons. The device contained only about 3.1 milligrams of it. These neutrons then travelled through 52 plates containing highly enriched uranium.
When neutrons struck some of the uranium atoms, the atoms split and released more neutrons. This process is called nuclear fission.
The arrangement allowed Kodak to produce a much larger supply of neutrons than californium alone could provide. According to the report, the number could increase by as much as 30 times.
But the machine could not keep this process going by itself. It depended on californium to supply the neutrons needed to start and maintain the reactions, or the reaction would gradually stop.
How did the public find out about the device?
Kodak operated the machine for more than three decades. During that period, its californium source was replaced approximately every seven years so the equipment could continue functioning.
The device was housed behind thick protective walls and operated under government-approved security arrangements. Although it was used for research, the company did not widely publicise its presence.
The story reached a much larger audience in 2012, when information about the facility appeared in local news reports.
According to an Associated Press report published in May 2012, Kodak's equipment contained about 3.5 pounds of highly enriched uranium. The report also confirmed that the machine had been used for examining materials and producing images.
By then, however, the device was no longer operating. Kodak had stopped using it in 2006, and the uranium was removed in 2007 during the dismantling process. The material was transferred to a federal facility under strict security arrangements.
The former laboratory was later declared safe, although small amounts of radioactive isotopes had been activated in the concrete surrounding the equipment. The building has since been sold by Kodak.
